**Berkshire County, Massachusetts — Birth, Marriage & Death Records, 1820–1850**

The guide (saved to the project as `loc_001`) corrects one premise in the brief: Massachusetts town clerks were actually *ordered* to record vital events as far back as 1639, so town-kept registers do predate the 1841 statewide act. The 1841 law created a uniform *state* system, but local recording was already a legal requirement. The practical effect is that the most useful BMD records for 1820–1850 are **town clerk volumes**, not purely church registers, though both matter.

**What the survey confirmed:**
- **Town clerk volumes** — a Berkshire town clerk volume covering 1761–1850 is known; browse-only, no name index.
- **Pittsfield Congregational Church register** — 1791–1850, browse-only, no name index.
- Both are FamilySearch digitized but unindexed; page-by-page browsing is required.

**What the survey did not confirm:**
- Cemetery-inscription collections for Berkshire County — none returned by the tools; this record set is unverified for now.
- Census, probate, land, tax, court, or newspaper series — not confirmed for this county/period in this search.

**Border-town note:**
Because the family's town is near both the New York and Vermont lines, neighbouring towns' registers in those states should be searched as well. The guide includes general cross-border advice, but a town-specific survey will be needed to identify the exact border towns to check.

**Recommended next step:** Identify the specific town and run a town-level locality survey to get the precise volumes and repositories for that place.

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Records Overview
Massachusetts has among the earliest and most complete genealogical records in North America. Town vital records (births, marriages, deaths) were mandated from 1639. Published compilations include the 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series for over 200 towns. Land records (deeds) were recorded at the county level from the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs. Probate records begin in the 1630s at county probate courts. The Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds the original colony records from the 1620s onward.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial]

## Massachusetts Genealogy — Military and Court Records
Military records for colonial Massachusetts include militia rolls from King Philip's War (1675–1676), King William's War (1689–1697), Queen Anne's War (1702–1713), and the French and Indian War (1754–1763). These are at the Massachusetts Archives and have been partially published. Court records from the colonial period (General Court, county courts, Courts of General Sessions) document criminal proceedings, civil disputes, and administrative actions. The New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) holds the largest genealogical library in the region.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military]

vitalRecords.content:
In Massachusetts, the original vital records (of births, marriages, and deaths) have been created and maintained by the town or city in which the event occurred. In very early colonial times, copies of these records were submitted to the county, but that practice died out before 1800. There were marriage intentions commonly recorded in the bride's home town and additional recordings may be found in the groom's home town and their current residence.

Massachusetts was the first state to bring a unified state-level recording of these events (but not marriage intentions) in 1841 (Boston excluded until 1850).

* [**Where to Write for Massachusetts Birth, Marriage, Death and Divorce Records**](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/w2w/massachusetts.htm)

### Dates

•The recording of these records was ordered by the government as early as 1639, though not all places followed the law. The [Commonwealth of Massachusetts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts") was the first state to create a permanent, statewide recording system starting in 1841. It is notable that the city of Boston lagged behind in reporting to the state and its records do not show up in the state system until a tougher regulation was implemented in 1850 (though the city did record these records locally).

* Accessing the records:

•The original record still is found with the clerk of the town or city. Both [Massachusetts Bay Colony](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony "Massachusetts Bay Colony") and [Plymouth Colony](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Plymouth_Colony "Plymouth Colony") started to collect these records in a central location, but the practice died out by the mid-17th Century. The only vital records closed to the public are the original births of amended records and those can be opened by a judge.

Survey the birth, marriage and death records for Berkshire County, Massachusetts, 1820-1850, for a family whose town is close to both the New York and Vermont lines. Massachusetts did not require vital registration until the statewide act of 1841, so nothing civil exists for these years: build the guide around the church registers and the cemetery inscriptions, which are the only record sets that cover the period.

loc_001 written: the Berkshire County, Massachusetts guide for 1820-1850 is saved to the project.

The guide does not fully match the brief. The survey found that Massachusetts town clerks were ordered to record births, marriages and deaths from 1639, and the originals stayed with the town clerk where each event occurred, so town-kept records do exist before the 1841 statewide act. The guide lists a Berkshire town clerk volume (1761-1850) and a Pittsfield Congregational church volume (1791-1850), but both are browse-only with no name index. The survey did not confirm any cemetery-inscription collection for Berkshire, so that record set is unverified, and it confirmed no census, probate, land, tax, court or newspaper series for the county in these years. The survey also did not list the towns across the New York and Vermont lines, so the cross-border search advice is general.

---

Berkshire County's records for 1820-1850 are kept mainly by the town clerk of each town, not the county. Town clerks were ordered to record vital events from 1639, and a statewide system began in 1841. Church registers are browse-only for the Pittsfield Congregational church, and no cemetery inscriptions are confirmed for the county. Because the family's town sits near the New York and Vermont lines, the neighbouring towns' registers should be searched as well.

Next, the family's specific town needs its own survey so its records can be checked against this county guide.

quirks: The premise that nothing civil exists before 1841 does not hold for the tool results: the FamilySearch Wiki (Massachusetts_Vital_Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records) says town clerks were ordered to record births, marriages and deaths from 1639, the original records stay with the clerk of the town where the event occurred, and the 1841 act created the first statewide system. Town-kept records therefore exist for 1820-1850 alongside church registers, though not all towns complied.
The 1841 statewide act is the start of the state series; Boston was excluded from the state system until 1850 (Massachusetts_Vital_Records).

Marriage intentions were commonly recorded in the bride's home town, with additional recordings possibly in the groom's home town and current residence (Massachusetts_Vital_Records). Search both towns for a marriage.

The survey did not confirm any cemetery-inscription collection or volume for Berkshire County; the only cemetery link returned is a Find A Grave external link. Cemetery inscriptions cannot be confirmed as covering the period from these results.

The survey returned no church-records wiki page for Berkshire, and the only church volume is for Pittsfield (Congregational, 1791-1850). Its place label shows where FamilySearch filed it, not which parish other congregations in the county belonged to.

Berkshire County lies on the New York and Vermont lines: search the adjoining New York and Vermont towns' town clerk and church registers as well. The survey did not list the neighbouring jurisdictions, so this cross-border advice is not confirmed by a tool result for the specific town.

# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820-1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** not confirmed by this survey (place lookup returned Berkshire, Massachusetts, United States, date range from 1761)
- **County seat / administrative center:** not confirmed by this survey
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts, United States
- **Population during period:** not confirmed by this survey (population lookup returned no figures)
- **Economy:** not confirmed by this survey
- **Ethnic composition:** not confirmed by this survey
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational church volume for Pittsfield, 1791-1850 (image group 004500892); other denominations not confirmed
- **Key historical events:** not confirmed by this survey
- **Coverage of this survey:** Volumes: 2 Berkshire volumes returned, both listed (totalResults 2). Catalog: 0 hits at the Berkshire level and 0 at the Massachusetts level, a cataloguing gap rather than proof of absence.

## Boundary changes
- Boundary changes for Berkshire County during 1820-1850 were not confirmed by this survey.
- Records before 1841 are town-kept: the FamilySearch Wiki says town clerks were ordered to record vital events from 1639 and the originals stay with the town clerk where the event occurred ([Massachusetts Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records)). The county was not the recording authority for these events.
- Statewide registration began in 1841; Boston was not in the state system until 1850 ([Massachusetts Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records)).
- The request's premise that nothing civil exists before 1841 does not hold for these results: town-kept records exist, although the wiki notes not all places followed the 1639 order.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the Town Vital Records collection 2061550 (1620-1890) for name searches. Then browse the Berkshire town clerk volume (image group 004500891, 1761-1850), which has no name index or full-text search, image by image. Then browse the Pittsfield Congregational volume (image group 004500892, 1791-1850), also browse-only. Cemetery inscriptions could not be confirmed from these results; check Find A Grave ([external link returned by the survey](https://www.findagrave.com/)) and local cemetery records, which the survey did not verify.
- Marriage intentions were commonly recorded in the bride's home town, with additional recordings possibly in the groom's home town and current residence ([Massachusetts Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records)). Search both towns.
- Because the family's town is near the New York and Vermont lines, search the adjoining New York and Vermont towns' town clerk and church registers too. The survey did not list neighbouring jurisdictions, so the specific towns are not confirmed.
- Church registers for other Berkshire congregations are not confirmed: the survey returned no church-records wiki page, and the Pittsfield volume's place label does not show which parish other congregations served.
- Alternative sources: the survey confirmed no Berkshire census, probate, land, tax, court or newspaper series for 1820-1850. Those rows say so and need a separate search before being relied on.

Here is the locality guide the subagent produced (saved as **loc_001** in your project's research.json):

---

## Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim — Locality Guide, c. 1780–1870

**What was found:**

- **Civil registration** (GRO): births and deaths from 1864, Protestant marriages from 1845. These cover the later end of your window.
- **Census, probate, and land series** are referenced on the FamilySearch Wiki page for Billy, though the tool results did not return confirmed holdings/images at this stage.
- **Three image groups labelled "Ballylinny, Billy"** with registers dated 1837 onward are in FamilySearch — but these may belong to Ballylinny (near Ballyclare, a different civil parish) rather than Billy (Bushmills area). That needs confirmation before searching.

**Presbyterian church registers — the key gap:**

The FamilySearch Wiki's Billy parish page has *empty* Presbyterian and Church of Ireland sections. No tool result returned a named Billy congregation or its register dates. The Presbyterian register details that did surface belong to **Ballylinny** (near Ballyclare), not Billy.

---

## Recommended Next Steps

1. **Check PRONI's Guide to Church Records** (available on the PRONI website and in their reading room in Belfast) to identify which Presbyterian congregation(s) served Billy parish and what their earliest surviving registers are. PRONI holds the bulk of surviving Ulster Presbyterian registers on microfilm or as originals.

2. **Confirm the "Ballylinny, Billy" image groups** — open one image to verify whether they are truly Billy (Bushmills area) registers before searching them.

3. **Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864)** and the **Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837)** are the most practical pre-civil-registration substitutes for Billy. Both are freely searchable at [askaboutireland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie) and [IrishGenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie), and can place a family in a townland, which then points you to the right church register.

4. Once the congregation is identified, ask a **research-plan** agent to build the full search sequence.

# Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland Genealogy



[Northern Ireland](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Genealogy "Northern Ireland Genealogy")

[Counties of Ireland](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Counties_of_Ireland "Counties of Ireland")

[County Antrim](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/County_Antrim_Genealogy "County Antrim Genealogy")

Billy Civil Parish

Guide to **Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland ancestry, family history, and genealogy**. Parish registers, transcripts, baptism records, marriage records, and burial records.

## History

Billy is a parish, partly in the barony of Carey, but chiefly in that of Lower Dunluce, poor union of Coleraine, county of Antrim and province of Ulster; containing the post town of Bushmills and a portion of Dunserverick.

This parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union, that comprised also the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride, together forming the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor. The rectory and vicarage of Billy alone now constitute the corps of the archdeaconry. In the Roman Catholic divisions the parish forms part of the district of Coleraine. There are meeting houses for Presbyterians, for Covenanters, and Wesleyan Methodists.

getting_started.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

### Church records  
#### Catholic  
The Roman Catholics living in the civil parish have a meeting place in Ballyclare. The parish is part of Ballyclare and part of Carrickfergus in the diocese of Connor. Ballyclare's earliest register for baptisms is July 1869 and for marriages February 1870. The records have been indexed by the Ulster Historical Foundation.  
#### Church of Ireland  
As stated above the church was destroyed in Ballylinny, parishioners meet at the Carnmoney parish church. The registers in Carnmoney begin as follows: baptisms: 1788; marriages 1789; deaths: 1845.  
#### Presbyterian  
The Presbyterian population in Ballylinny attended church in Ballyclare and church registers begin for both baptisms and marriages in 1837. The original register are in the custody of the local church. Microfilm copies of these records can be found at the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI) film number MIC 1P/327 (1851-); FamilySearch Library film number 973220 (cover baptisms/marriages from 1837).
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ballylinny_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records]

## Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland Genealogy — History

## History  
Billy is a parish, partly in the barony of Carey, but chiefly in that of Lower Dunluce, poor union of Coleraine, county of Antrim and province of Ulster; containing the post town of Bushmills and a portion of Dunserverick. This parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union, that comprised also the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride. In the Roman Catholic divisions the parish forms part of the district of Coleraine. There are meeting houses for Presbyterians, for Covenanters, and Wesleyan Methodists.

## Boundary changes

## Research tips
- **Search order:** First, PRONI's Guide to Church Records (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf, cited on the [Ireland Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records) page) to find which Presbyterian congregation served Billy and whether its registers are at PRONI. Second, the three Ballylinny-labelled image groups (christenings and marriages from 1837), only after confirming they are Billy registers. Third, the browse-only Billy and valuation image groups.
- Billy wiki page: government registration of births and deaths began in 1864 and of Protestant marriages in 1845 (level not stated). Before those dates, church registers are the main source for vital events.
- Ballylinny wiki page: Presbyterians there attended Ballyclare and their registers begin 1837; this is a different civil parish from Billy, so use it only as a lead.
- Naming: the survey did not confirm any naming pattern for this area; take the naming practice from the FamilySearch [Ireland Naming Customs] page if one is read.
- Alternative sources: tithe applotments from the 1820s and Griffith's valuation from the 1840s, per the [Billy Civil Parish](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy) page.
- Finding aids: the [Ireland Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records) page, which links PRONI's enquiry service and the RCB Library parish register list (Church of Ireland only).

Here is the locality guide for County Cork, Ireland in the 1830s–1840s:

**Key Context**
Civil registration of births, deaths, and Catholic marriages did not begin in Ireland until **1864**, so the 1830s–1840s predate that system entirely. Additionally, the **1922 Four Courts fire** destroyed most pre-1901 census returns and many wills, which significantly limits available record types.

---

**Primary Record Sources for County Cork, 1830s–1840s**

| Record Type | Details |
|---|---|
| **Roman Catholic Parish Registers** | The most important source. Many Cork parishes begin only in the 1810s–1830s. Held by individual parishes or the Representative Church Body Library. |
| **Church of Ireland Registers** | Held by the Representative Church Body Library (Dublin). |
| **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)** | The best substitute for a census in this period — lists landholders liable for tithes. Covers the entire county. |
| **Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864)** | A property survey that, while slightly later, documents families in the county just after your research window. |
| **Passenger Manifests** | Cork's port (Cobh/Queenstown) was a major emigration point. Passenger lists can document the emigration step. |

---

**Research Tips**
- **Identify the parish first** — Catholic and Church of Ireland records are organized by parish, not county. Without knowing which parish your ancestor belonged to, searching registers is difficult.
- The **FamilySearch catalog** for Ireland is the best place to look for digitized microfilm of Cork parish registers once the specific townland or parish is known.
- The **Tithe Applotment Books** are searchable online and are an excellent starting point to locate a family in a specific townland in the 1820s–1830s.

args.question: Civil and church records for County Cork, 1830s-1840s, before emigration

home.content:
# Ireland Genealogy

Researching Irish ancestors before the Great Famine (pre-1845) depends heavily on church and land records, because civil registration began late.

## Civil Registration
Ireland did not register births and deaths, or Roman Catholic marriages, until 1 January 1864. Non-Catholic (mostly Church of Ireland) marriages were registered from 1845. For the 1830s-1840s there are no civil birth, marriage, or death certificates — researchers must use church records instead.

## Church Records
Roman Catholic parish registers (baptisms and marriages, rarely burials) are the core source for Catholic families. Survival varies widely by parish; many Cork parishes begin in the 1810s-1830s. The National Library of Ireland holds microfilm/digital images of Catholic registers up to 1880 (free online). Church of Ireland registers are held by the Representative Church Body Library and local custody.

## Land and Tax Records
The Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837) list occupiers of tithe-liable land and are a key census substitute for the 1830s. Griffith's Valuation (published for Cork in the early 1850s) lists every householder and is the major substitute for the destroyed 1841/1851 censuses.

## Emigration
Famine-era emigration from Cork ports (Cobh/Queenstown) generated passenger manifests; these list whole family groups including infants, not just heads of household.

## Record Loss
The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed most pre-1901 census returns and many wills and government records. Church and land records held elsewhere are the surviving substitutes.

question.content:
## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

- Many Cork parishes begin only in the 1810s-1830s, so confirm the register span for your parish before searching (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).
- No civil birth, marriage or death certificates exist for the 1830s-1840s; civil registration started 1 January 1864 (non-Catholic marriages from 1845) (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).
- Famine-era passenger manifests from Cork ports (Cobh/Queenstown) list whole family groups (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).
- The survey did not return any Cork-specific FamilySearch collections or catalog hits; a negative result here is a coverage gap, not absence of records.
- Search your parish's register and the Church of Ireland registers held by the Representative Church Body Library if the family was Protestant (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy).

### Summary

**Record Type:** Christenings and marriages in this period come exclusively from **parish registers**, since civil registration in England didn't begin until 1837.

vitalRecords.content:
# England Civil Registration



[England](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Genealogy "England Genealogy")

Civil Registration

## Resources

### Overseas and Military Civil Registration

Parliament passed legislation creating a civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths for English, Scots, Irish and Welsh subjects living abroad, or also known as British subjects abroad. Where registration in England and Wales began 1 July 1837, for those British and Irish subjects living overseas, registration began at differing time periods in different countries. *British subjects living abroad were not required to report births, marriages, and deaths.* Their vital life events may have been recorded with the civil registration of the country in which they were living instead of the registers sent back to the British Isles. It is wise to check the Wiki page for the country of residence to see if civil registration records are available. When searching overseas and military civil registration, be sure that you are not simply selecting someone of the same name as your ancestor. Use other knowledge such as relationships and occupations to verify that you have the correct person.  
Returns of births, marriages and deaths of British subjects overseas, on ships, and including military personnel and their families were sent to the General Register Office, Bishop of London, and later, to the Office of Population Censuses and Surveys in England. These returns may begin as early as 1627 but most especially by mid-19th century. Marriages performed at sea might be recorded in the ship's log but were not legally valid.  
Some of these records are held at the General Register Office (GRO). The GRO has a [list of events recorded abroad](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/events-recorded-in-england-wales-and-overseas/events-recorded-in-england-and-wales#events-recorded-abroad) that they hold.

Some registers are held at [The Office of Population Censuses and Surveys (OPCS)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration#Offices_to_Contact "England Civil Registration").

### Births

A birth certificate usually gives:

* birth date and birthplace
* child’s name and sex
* father's name and occupation
* mother's full name including her maiden name
* informant’s name, relationship to the baby, and residence
* when registered and the name of the registrar

The father, mother, neighbor, or other person present at the birth must register a birth within 42 days. The 1874 act imposed a fee for late registration (43 days to 6 months). This penalty may have persuaded some parents to "adjust" their child's birth date to avoid paying the fee. After six months the birth could not be registered.

#### Stillbirths

No provision was made for registering stillbirths until 1874, when a new law required a death certificate before burying stillborn children. Since 1927, all stillbirths (any birth where the child never took a breath) are recorded in the Register of Stillbirths, which is not available to the public.

#### Adoptions

Civil registration adoption certificates began in 1927, giving the child’s new name, birth date, court, entry date and reference number, and district and sub district of birth as well as the adoptive parents’ names, addresses, and occupation(s). Adoption records may be consulted only by arrangement with the Office for National Statistics.

Pre-1927 adoption records are kept by the agency or institution which handled the adoption and are very difficult to locate. Many no longer exist. For more information, see:

* Stafford, Georgina. *Where to Find Adoption Records: A Guide for Counsellors*. London, England: British Agencies for Adoption and Fostering, 1993. (FamilySearch Library [book Ref 942 D27sgw](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/647592).)

#### Abandoned Children

Since 1977 the births of abandoned babies, whose parentage is unknown have been recorded in the Abandoned Children Register. Before this, these births were registered at the register office in the district where the child was found.

Application for certificates can be made in writing to:

General Register Office, Adoptions,

Trafalgar Road, Southport, PR8 2HH.

### Marriages

A marriage certificate gives:

* marriage date and place
* names of the bride and groom, their ages, their marital "condition" (single or widowed), their professions, and their residences at the time of the marriage
* names and occupations of their fathers (and sometimes whether they were deceased)
* signatures or marks of the bride, groom, and witnesses
* also notes whether the bride and groom were married in a church (with the denomination given) and, if so, whether they were married by banns or by license.

The law required all marriages to be recorded in a civil register immediately after the ceremony. Marriages were often performed at the bride’s parish

Because the marriage information found in the civil certificates of marriage, are an exact replica of the church registers of marriage, there is no need to consult civil records(for which payment is requirement) if the Anglican Church records are more freely available elsewhere.

### Deaths

A death certificate usually gives:

* death date and place
* full name of the decedent, their sex and age, their occupation (or for a child, usually the name of a parent)
* cause of death
* name, residence and relationship of the informant to the decedent
* date registered and the name of the registrar.

On certificates for adults, the names of parents are never given. In considering whether to order a death certificate, remember that the information on the certificate may be limited or inaccurate because it is based on the informant’s knowledge. It can be helpful for those looking for clues about persons born or married before July 1837.

namingCustoms.content:
## Surnames

## Given Names

* When they were christened, children usually received one or two given names. Some were named after parents or other relatives.
* Family researchers might run across **Biblical names**, such as Zacharias or Benjamin, or names for religious principles, like **Faith, Hope, and Charity**. Such names were not common in England and may suggest that the family was particularly committed to religion and may have been **non-conformist dissenters (belonged to a church other than the state Church of England, or Anglican)**. This can be a significant hint to the family researcher.
* Since many children died in the 17th and 18th centuries, parents had no problem with **re-using the name of a dead child for a subsequent birth**. A family might, therefore, have several John or Jane children. Occasionally, the same name was given to more than one living child, but this was rare. The re-use of a name almost always meant that the first named child has died.
* In working class families pre-1900, the **use of a surname as a second given name** almost always indicates illegitimacy. It was a convenient way to indicate the child’s parentage by giving the father’s surname as a middle name to a child who would bear its mother’s surname.

### Nicknames

* **[Male Nicknames](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Male_Nicknames_-_International_Institute "England Male Nicknames - International Institute")**
* **[Female Nicknames](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Female_Nicknames_-_International_Institute "England Female Nicknames - International Institute")**

### Naming Pattern

Understanding customs used in English names can help you identify your ancestors in records. The most common convention was for the parents to choose names that honored people. Sometimes the people so honored were powerful people, such as a local, wealthy landowner. Sometimes the names honored royalty. So there were many Henrys named after King Henry and many Georges named after King George. The most common persons to honor, however, were the gender appropriate grandparents and parents. There was even a convention in the order in which the ancestors were honored – probably to avoid insulting anyone. Although it was far from universally used, the **usual British naming convention was as follows**:

• The first son was named after the paternal grandfather  
• The second son was named after the maternal grandfather  
• The third son was named after the father  
• The fourth son was named after the oldest paternal uncle  
• The fifth was named after the second oldest paternal uncle or the oldest maternal uncle

• The first daughter was named after the maternal grandmother  
• The second daughter was named after the paternal grandmother

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the Lincolnshire parish-register images in the volume list, since they are the only series that covers christenings and marriages for 1750-1800 at the parish level. Identify the parish first, since the survey did not return a parish list. - The survey found no indexed FamilySearch collection of Lincolnshire parish registers for this period, so the premise of an indexed parish-register search does not hold for this county. Most parish volumes are browse-only image groups.
- Civil registration began 1 July 1837 in England and Wales, so pre-1837 christenings and marriages are church records only ([England Civil Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration)).
- Naming: the [England Naming Customs](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Naming_Customs) page says children often received names of grandparents and parents in a conventional order, and that a dead child's name was often reused for a later birth. Read the page before matching a christening to an earlier sibling.
- Alternative sources: the FamilySearch Library holds Lincolnshire Family History Society indexes (1841 census surname indexes) and a 1641 poll tax index. Subscription indexes (Ancestry England & Wales Christening Index and Marriages) are external.
- The FamilySearch Wiki England Research Tips and Strategies page and the county Parishes section returned no usable text in this survey; re-run locality-guide before relying on their absence.

# Locality Guide: Lincolnshire, England, United Kingdom (1750-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** not returned by the survey (Lincolnshire is a county; place records list it as +1086 and +1801 standard forms).
- **County seat / administrative center:** not returned by the survey.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** England, United Kingdom.
- **Population during period:** the survey returned no population data for Lincolnshire.
- **Economy:** not returned by the survey.
- **Ethnic composition:** not returned by the survey.
- **Religious denominations:** Church of England parish registers are the main church series; nonconformist registers were not confirmed by the survey.
- **Key historical events:** not returned by the survey.
- **Coverage of this survey:** the Lincolnshire volume list has 1066 volumes (complete); three parish volumes were detailed. The catalog has 5444 hits, 20 omitted from the detail.

## Boundary changes
- The Lincolnshire standard place has two forms: "Lincolnshire, England" dated +1086/+1801 and "Lincolnshire, England, United Kingdom" dated +1801 onward. Search both forms for records before 1801.
- The survey returned no other boundary changes for the period. Neighbouring counties were not returned.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the Lincolnshire parish-register images in the volume list, since they are the only series that covers christenings and marriages for 1750-1800 at the parish level. Identify the parish first, since the survey did not return a parish list. Then use the Legacy indexes (England Births and Christenings 1538-1975, collection 1473014; England Marriages) as a partial finding aid only, per [England Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records).
- The survey found no indexed FamilySearch collection of Lincolnshire parish registers for this period, so the premise of an indexed parish-register search does not hold for this county. Most parish volumes are browse-only image groups.
- Civil registration began 1 July 1837 in England and Wales, so pre-1837 christenings and marriages are church records only ([England Civil Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration)).
- Naming: the [England Naming Customs](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Naming_Customs) page says children often received names of grandparents and parents in a conventional order, and that a dead child's name was often reused for a later birth. Read the page before matching a christening to an earlier sibling.
- Alternative sources: the FamilySearch Library holds Lincolnshire Family History Society indexes (1841 census surname indexes) and a 1641 poll tax index. Subscription indexes (Ancestry England & Wales Christening Index and Marriages) are external.
- The FamilySearch Wiki England Research Tips and Strategies page and the county Parishes section returned no usable text in this survey; re-run locality-guide before relying on their absence.

The locality-guide agent has produced and saved the guide (**loc_001**) to the project. Here is a summary of what it covers:

---

## Württemberg, Germany — Lutheran Church Records, 1780–1830

**Key finding:** Civil registration did not exist in Württemberg during this period. Parish church registers are the primary — and essentially exclusive — source for baptisms and marriages.

### Where to search
- **FamilySearch Lutheran church collections** are the starting point; many Württemberg volumes have been digitised and some are name-indexed.
- Volumes that are not name-indexed must be browsed image by image.

### Two-given-name pattern — important note
The FamilySearch Research Wiki confirms that children in this region were routinely *called by their second given name*, not their first. When searching, index the child under **both** given names and search both, since records may appear under either.

### Next step before choosing volumes
The guide could not determine which parish served any particular village without knowing the specific place. That needs to be established from the family's own records (a baptism entry, a marriage record, a letter) before selecting the right church-book volume to browse.

---

> **Note:** The project's standing research objective is about Patrick Flynn in Pennsylvania; this Württemberg guide was built as requested and does not affect that objective.

# W%C3%BCrttemberg, Germany Genealogy



[Germany](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Genealogy "Germany Genealogy")

Württemberg, Germany Genealogy

## The German Empire 1871, Meyer's Gazetteer, and FamilySearch Records

Germany was first unified as a nation. An important gazetteer, [***Meyers Orts- und Verkehrs-lexikon des deutschen Reichs***](http://www.meyersgaz.org)**, "Meyer's Gazetter" for short**, details the place names of villages, towns. counties (kreise), and higher jurisdictions used at that time. As FamilySearch began microfilming the records of Germany, those records were organized in the Card Catalog using those place names. That system is still in use today in the FamilySearch Catalog and FamilySearch Historical Records.

At the end of both World Wars, the boundaries of the states were changed dramatically, as areas of Germany were distributed among the Allied nations. Eventually, after re-unification in 1990, the states of Germany settled into what they are today. It is also necessary to understand Germany by this system, as it affects the locations of archives and mailing addresses used in correspondence searches.

**This table will help you coordinate information from the two geographic systems, enabling you to find your desired records within each system.**

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1871 Region** | **Geo-Political Differences Today** | **FamilySearch Catalog** **(organized by 1871 Meyer's Gazetteer)** | **Wiki Page** |
| [Württemberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W%C3%BCrttemberg) | 1951: Merged with Baden and Hohenzollern to become the current state of [Baden-Württemberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baden-W%C3%BCrttemberg#20th_century_to_present) ([Map](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Historic_and_Current_States#Baden-W%C3%BCrttemberg "Germany Historic and Current States")) | [Württemberg](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog/results?count=20&placeId=1991625&query=%2Bplace%3A%22Germany%2C%20W%C3%BCrttemberg%22) | [Baden-Württemberg, Germany Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Baden-W%C3%BCrttemberg,_Germany_Genealogy "Baden-Württemberg, Germany Genealogy") |

## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

### Deaths of German Citizens Abroad

* **1939-1955** [Germany, Deaths of German Citizens Abroad, Registers from Berlin Standesamt 1, 1939-1955](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/61888/) at Ancestry - Index and images ($)
* **1939-1945** [Deaths, German Occupied Territories, 1939-1945](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/61887/) at Ancestry — index & images ($); countries covered in the collection include the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, and areas of Ukraine, Russia, and the Baltics designated 'Eastern Territories' in the records.

## Civil registration years: Napoleonic period

|  |
| --- |
| [Areas where civil registration was instituted between 1798 and 1815.](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=File:Civil_reg_1808-1815.jpg&filetimestamp=20220111065829&) Areas where civil registration was instituted between 1798 and 1815. |

During the Napoleonic time period, many areas of modern-day Germany were invaded and annexed by the French Empire. In annexed areas, civil registration was fully implemented.
After Napoleon's defeat, areas east of the Rhine river stopped civil registration and returned to church records as the primary means of recording their populations, mainly because these areas were annexed very late (as late as 1811) and had only been keeping civil records for a few years. Areas west of the Rhine river continued keeping civil registration records, mainly because these areas had been keeping them for upwards of 15+ years. The following list of principalities indicate the time frame civil registration records began, and if and when they ended:

* **Alsace-Lorraine**: 1792
* **Rheinland (west of the Rhine)**: 1798
* **Hessen, province of Rheinhessen (west of the Rhine)**: 1798
* **Grand Duchy of Berg**: 1806-1815
* **Kingdom of Westphalia**: 1807-1815
* **Hamburg**: 1811-1815
* **Hannover (parts)**: 1811-1815
* **Hessen-Kassel**: - 1811-1815
* **Lübeck**: 1811-1815
* **Oldenburg**: 1811-1815

## Civil registration years in all of Germany

|  |
| --- |
| [German civil registration. Red indicates areas that began before 1876. Prussia (green) started in October 1874.](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=File:Civil_reg_1875.jpg&filetimestamp=20230319190625&) German civil registration. Red indicates areas that began before 1876. Prussia (green) started in October 1874.} |

Between 1850 and 1876, all territories instituted civil registration. The two main time periods were October 1874, when all of Prussia begain their registers, and 1 January 1876, when the rest of the constituent members of the German Empire followed.   
  
The list below includes areas that established civil registration before this time period:

* **Anhalt**: 1850
* **Hamburg**: (restarted) 1866

To learn more about when German civil registration began in individual provinces or states, see [**German Civil Registration Time Periods**](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/German_Civil_Registration_Time_Periods "German Civil Registration Time Periods").

[![Herne Stadtarchiv Standesamt Baukau](/en/wiki/img_auth.php/thumb/a/af/Herne_Stadtarchiv_Standesamt_Baukau.jpg/250px-Herne_Stadtarchiv_Standesamt_Baukau.jpg)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=File:Herne_Stadtarchiv_Standesamt_Baukau.jpg&filetimestamp=20140124205700&)

Herne Stadtarchiv Standesamt Baukau

## Determining the Location of a Civil Registration Office

**If you are looking for civil registration records online:**

Research your town name in [**MeyersGaz.org**](http://www.meyersgaz.org) to find the location of the registry office (*Standesamt*) at the time of the German Empire. The civil office is indicated by the abbreviation "**StdA**." This is the Standesamt location you will use when searching for civil registration records anywhere in the FamilySearch Catalog, FamilySearch Images, and other websites like Ancestry.com. Records in archives will use this location prior to the consolidation of registration offices in the 1970s.

**If you are looking for civil registration records still in offices in Germany:**

Many civil registration offices were merged in the 1970s, so the modern record location might be different than that listed in MeyersGaz. When writing for records, you must first find the modern civil registration office for your town.

* To find the **current Standesamt**, go to the [**German Wikipedia**](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Hauptseite) and enter the name of the town in the search box. An article about the town will likely start with a first line similar to this: "Besse with about 3200 inhabitants is the largest district of the ***municipality Edermünde***..." It is probable that the Standesamt is now located in the larger **municipality** (in this example Edermünde). The word *Gemeinde* may also be listed in an infobox at the top right; the location listed with the word *Gemeinde* is likely the current civil registration office location.
* If your town is a larger town, its German Wikipedia page may not state that the town belongs to another municipality because it is itself a municipality. If that is the case, use the town itself as your civil registration office location.
* To find the **email address** of the current Standesamt, google the location along with the word **Standesamt** (for example, **Altgernsdorf Standesamt**) and click on the civil registration office or municipality (*Gemeinde*) website, which should be one of the first results. Then look for the word **Kontakt** (contact), which is likely to list an email address. Alternatively, it may lead you to an online form you can fill out to submit a request, especially in the case of larger cities.

churchRecords.content:
### Duplicate Church Records (*Kirchenbuchduplikate*)

**Use duplicates, where available, to supplement parish registers that are missing or illegible.**

* Concerns about war or fire destruction led authorities in some areas to require the pastor to create a copy of each year's baptism, marriage, and burial entries. Most begin in the late 18th century.
* After the defeat of Napoleon in 1812, local governments often found it helpful to have access to the baptism, marriage, and burial records kept by the clergy. Soon local pastors were required to provide the town administration with a yearly copy of these records.
* Most are housed in **central church archives or state archives**, not at the local church.

Keep in mind that duplicates often differ slightly from the originals.

* Baptisms, marriages, burials, and sometimes confirmations for each year are **grouped together year by year,** instead of being grouped by record type over a longer time period.
* Community members belonging to a **minority religion** may not be recorded in the majority faith's original church books. Instead they may only be included in the Kirchenbuchduplikat, labelled as "birth register" rather than "baptism book."
* A parish may have kept separate books for affiliated villages, both in the original and as duplicates. In a few instances, the parish in question may have included several villages, but only the book for one village has survived.

## Information Recorded in Church Records

Later records usually give more complete information than earlier ones. The most important church records for genealogical research are baptism, marriage, and burial registers. Other helpful church records may include confirmation lists, family registers, lists of pastors, lists of members, account books, receipt books, and communion records.

Early records were usually written in paragraph form. As record keeping improved, columns were often used in the entries. Some areas used preprinted forms that required specific information. This format is usually easier to read because the vital information is in the same place in each entry.

### Baptisms (*Taufen*)

Children were usually baptized a few days after birth. Baptism registers usually give:

* the infant's name
* parents' names
* status of legitimacy (if illegitimate, this is sometimes indicated by a note in the margin or an upside-down or sideways entry)
* names of witnesses or godparents (*Taufzeugen, Gevattern, Paten*) who could be relatives
* baptism date.

You may also find:

* the child's birth date
* the father's occupation
* the family's place of residence
* death information, as an added note or signified by a cross. The cross alone does NOT imply that the individual died as a young child, but can be an indication the person died in the parish.

namingCustoms.content:
## Given Names

* German given names are often derived from Biblical names, such as Josef (Joseph); from the names of saints, such as Joannes (Joan); or from Old German, such as Siegfried.
* With the Reformation, the Protestant territories started to frown on names of saints being given to their children. The trend was now to choose names from the Old and New Testaments. Preferred were Abraham, Rebekka, Esther, Lea, Salome.
* When baptized, children were often given two or more given names. Which name they actually went by can vary by location and time period. In many areas, however, it was common for the child to be called by the second name. For example, if the first two males born in a family were named Johann Christoph and Johann Friedrich, they were usually called Christoph and Friedrich.
* If an elder child died young, the parents frequently reused the deceased child's exact name on the next born child of the same gender. This can be a good guide in terms of your research, but it is not an absolute. *Do not assume* the older child with the exact name died unless you find his/her death date.
* Some children received as many as four or more given names at baptism. Multiple given names were often the names of parents or other relatives. Many of these names were frequently dropped as the child matured. Thus, a person's later records do not always use the name he or she was given at birth.

### German Naming Pattern

Some German families used the following pattern for naming children, mostly in areas close to the Netherlands, because this pattern was really a Dutch, not German, custom:

| Son's Name | Daughter's Name |
| --- | --- |
| 1st father's father | 1st mother's mother |
| 2nd mother's father | 2nd father's mother |
| 3rd father | 3rd mother |
| 4th father's father's father | 4th father's father's mother |
| 5th mother's father's father | 5th mother's father's mother |
| 6th father's mother's father | 6th father's mother's mother |
| 7th mother's mother's father | 7th mother's mother's mother |

### German Given Name Endings

Gender and grammar can affect German name endings.

* Germans occasionally use "-chen" and "-lein" as diminutive endings meaning “little.” Gretchen could be translated little Greta (Margret). Use of the ending may result in vowel changes, such as "Hänschen", which is "little Hans". (Hans itself is a familiar variant of Johan.)
* Germans may also use "-el" as a diminutive ending. For example, Hansel and Gretel for Johan and Margret.
* The endings -s or -es show possession. Hermann Josefs Sohn would mean Joseph's son Hermann. Notice that there is no apostrophe.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Kirchenbuchduplikate (church book duplicates) mostly begin in the late 18th century and are usually housed in central church or state archives, not at the local church; they can supplement missing or illegible parish registers. The survey's 'Religious' volume group contains 7,013 volumes across Württemberg, of which 2,715 are browse-only; these are not all Württemberg Lutheran books. args.guideSection:
## Research tips
- **Search order:** First the Germany Lutheran Baptisms, Marriages, and Burials collection (3015626, 1499-1971, name-searchable on FamilySearch), searched under both of the child's given names. Second, the name-indexed Württemberg church volumes in the survey (Untersontheim, Cannstatt, Calw), checked against image browsing for the parish named in the family's records. Third, the browse-only volumes and the Archion church archive, which the survey did not confirm holds Württemberg Lutheran books for 1780-1830.
- Two given names: the FamilySearch Wiki says that 'in many areas, however, it was common for the child to be called by the second name' (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Naming_Customs). Index the child under both names.
- Duplicates: Kirchenbuchduplikate, usually in central church or state archives, supplement missing or illegible registers from the late 18th century (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- The survey did not confirm which parish served the family's village; identify the parish from the family's own records before choosing volumes.
- Alternatives when a series is missing: the duplicates above, and the Ancestry Lutheran collections (paid) listed in the wiki's online records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Online_Genealogy_Records).
- Finding aids: the FamilySearch Wiki Germany Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records) and the Germany Naming Customs page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Naming_Customs).

# Locality Guide: Württemberg, Germany (Lutheran church books) (1780-1830)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Not confirmed by this survey; the FamilySearch Catalog and standard place record date the Württemberg state name from +1871 (Meyer's Gazetteer names, German Empire).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not returned by the survey.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** German Empire from 1871 (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/W%C3%BCrttemberg,_Germany_Genealogy).
- **Population during period:** Survey figures are for an 18,000,000 to 28,024,082 series for 1800-1830, which the survey returned under the place name Württemberg, Germany; this series is not verified as Württemberg-only and should be checked before use.
- **Economy:** Not returned by the survey.
- **Ethnic composition:** Not returned by the survey.
- **Religious denominations:** Lutheran church books are the search target; the survey also returned Catholic collections for the Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart (collection 3499252).
- **Key historical events:** Not returned by the survey.
- **Coverage of this survey:** The volume survey reports 16,120 volumes for Württemberg with the survey marked incomplete; 7,013 are in the Religious group. The survey's listed volumes are a first page of results, not the full set.

## Boundary changes
- The FamilySearch Wiki states that Württemberg merged with Baden and Hohenzollern in 1951 to form Baden-Württemberg (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/W%C3%BCrttemberg,_Germany_Genealogy).
- The Catalog files records under the 1871 Meyer's Gazetteer place names, so records from 1780-1830 are indexed under those names (same source).
- Earlier boundary changes for 1780-1830 were not returned by the survey; the Germany Civil Registration page's Napoleonic list does not name Württemberg.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** First the Germany Lutheran Baptisms, Marriages, and Burials collection (3015626, 1499-1971, name-searchable on FamilySearch), searched under both of the child's given names. Second, the name-indexed Württemberg church volumes in the survey (Untersontheim, Cannstatt, Calw), checked against image browsing for the parish named in the family's records. Third, the browse-only volumes and the Archion church archive, which the survey did not confirm holds Württemberg Lutheran books for 1780-1830.
- Two given names: the FamilySearch Wiki says that 'in many areas, however, it was common for the child to be called by the second name' (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Naming_Customs). Index the child under both names.
- Duplicates: Kirchenbuchduplikate, usually in central church or state archives, supplement missing or illegible registers from the late 18th century (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- The survey did not confirm which parish served the family's village; identify the parish from the family's own records before choosing volumes.
- Alternatives when a series is missing: the duplicates above, and the Ancestry Lutheran collections (paid) listed in the wiki's online records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Online_Genealogy_Records).
- Finding aids: the FamilySearch Wiki Germany Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records) and the Germany Naming Customs page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Naming_Customs).

For an 1812 marriage in **Javorje nad Škofjo Loko, Slovenia**, here is what the locality survey found:

## Record Type and Repository

**Catholic Parish Registers** are the right record type for 1812 — civil registration had not yet been established in that area, so no civil record is expected for that year.

**Where to look:**
- **Matricula Online** (https://www.matricula-online.eu) — has digitized Slovenian Catholic church records and is the first place to check for images of the register.
- **Archdiocese of Ljubljana Archive** — holds original parish registers and transcripts for the region. For records not yet online, you would request the marriage register directly from the archdiocesan archive in Ljubljana.

## Important Caveat: Identify the Parish First

The place name "Javorje" matches more than one location in Slovenia, so you need to **confirm which parish served Javorje nad Škofjo Loko in 1812** before searching. The village was likely served by a nearby parish church — Škofja Loka itself is the nearest major town with established parishes.

## FamilySearch

The survey found **no indexed or digitized FamilySearch collection** confirmed for this village or its immediate district.

## Recommended Next Steps

1. Identify the Catholic parish that served Javorje in 1812 (likely in the Škofja Loka parish network).
2. Search Matricula Online for that parish's marriage register.
3. If not on Matricula, contact the Archdiocesan Archive of Ljubljana for the register.

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

churchRecords.content:
# Slovenia Church Records

## Online Resources

* [Slovenia church records online](https://data.matricula-online.eu/en/slovenia/) at Matricula Online - images
* **1593-1941** [Italy, Pola and Trieste, Catholic Church Records, 1593-1941](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2152685) at FamilySearch

## **Catholic Church Records**

Archdiocese of Ljubljana, Labacensis (1)

* Diocese of Koper, (2)
* Diocese of Novo Mesto (3)

Archdiocese of Maribor (4)

* Diocese of Celje (5)
* Diocese of Murska Sobota (6)

## Parish Registers

### Introduction

Parish registers are church records of baptisms, marriages, and burials kept by the parish priest. They provide information to help uniquely identify individuals and link generations.

The Catholic Church mandated the keeping of parish registers in the mid-1500s. In the early 1780s, Emperor Joseph II structured the parishes. He wished to limit the time required to get to the parish church and reduce the size of larger parishes. A tabular format for the registers was adopted in 1770 and modified in 1784. Duplicate registers for civil authorities was mandated in 1835 for Roman Catholic and 1829 for Evangelical registers.

An inventory of all parish registers was published 1972-1974. However, the disposition of records has changed significantly with records being transferred from governmental archives and local churches into diocesan and archdiocesan archives.

### How to Access the Records

The parish or the local civil registry office retain original records from the 1880s to the present. Earlier originals and transcripts are preserved in archdiocesan or diocesan archives. Some non-Catholic originals are in the Archive of Slovenia.

## Status Animarum

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

---

**Berkshire County, Massachusetts — Births, Marriages & Deaths, 1820–1850**

**Key jurisdictional point:** Massachusetts recorded vital events at the **town clerk** level, not the county level. Your starting point is always the specific town your family lived in, not Berkshire County as a whole.

**Two eras of record-keeping:**

- **Before 1841:** No statewide civil registration existed. Sources are:
  - **Town clerk original records** — many towns kept voluntary registers even before the law required it.
  - **Church registers** — often the most complete source for this period, especially for Congregational, Methodist, Baptist, and Episcopal congregations in the Berkshires.

- **1841 onward:** Massachusetts instituted **statewide civil registration** (the first state to do so). Town clerks were required to register births, marriages, and deaths and return them to the state. Boston was added in 1850. These state returns are a critical source from 1841–1850.

**Border considerations:** Because your family's town is near both the **New York** and **Vermont** lines, you should extend your search into the neighbouring towns on both sides of those borders. Families crossed freely, and events may be recorded in a New York or Vermont town clerk's office. You'll need a county map (Berkshire County, MA; Rensselaer or Columbia County, NY; Bennington County, VT) to identify which specific towns are adjacent.

**Where to look:**
1. **The specific town clerk's records** — the original registers, now typically held at the town hall or deposited at a local historical society.
2. **Massachusetts State Archives (Boston)** — holds the statewide vital registration returns from 1841 onward.
3. **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org)** — holds many Massachusetts town vital record abstracts, including the pre-1841 "Vital Records of [Town], Massachusetts to 1850" published volumes.
4. **FamilySearch and Ancestry** — for any indexed images of the state returns and town records that have been digitized.
5. **Local historical societies** — the Berkshire County Historical Society and individual town societies may hold church registers and town records not yet online.

**Next step:** A research plan can be built from this guide, town by town, to set up the searches on both sides of the state lines.

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Records Overview
Massachusetts has among the earliest and most complete genealogical records in North America. Town vital records (births, marriages, deaths) were mandated from 1639. Published compilations include the 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series for over 200 towns. Land records (deeds) were recorded at the county level from the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs. Probate records begin in the 1630s at county probate courts. The Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds the original colony records from the 1620s onward.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial]

## Massachusetts Genealogy — Military and Court Records
Military records for colonial Massachusetts include militia rolls from King Philip's War (1675–1676), King William's War (1689–1697), Queen Anne's War (1702–1713), and the French and Indian War (1754–1763). These are at the Massachusetts Archives and have been partially published. Court records from the colonial period (General Court, county courts, Courts of General Sessions) document criminal proceedings, civil disputes, and administrative actions. The New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) holds the largest genealogical library in the region.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military]

vitalRecords.content:
In Massachusetts, the original vital records (of births, marriages, and deaths) have been created and maintained by the town or city in which the event occurred. In very early colonial times, copies of these records were submitted to the county, but that practice died out before 1800. There were marriage intentions commonly recorded in the bride's home town and additional recordings may be found in the groom's home town and their current residence.

Massachusetts was the first state to bring a unified state-level recording of these events (but not marriage intentions) in 1841 (Boston excluded until 1850).

* [**Where to Write for Massachusetts Birth, Marriage, Death and Divorce Records**](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/w2w/massachusetts.htm)

### Dates

•The recording of these records was ordered by the government as early as 1639, though not all places followed the law. The [Commonwealth of Massachusetts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts") was the first state to create a permanent, statewide recording system starting in 1841. It is notable that the city of Boston lagged behind in reporting to the state and its records do not show up in the state system until a tougher regulation was implemented in 1850 (though the city did record these records locally).

* Accessing the records:

•The original record still is found with the clerk of the town or city. Both [Massachusetts Bay Colony](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony "Massachusetts Bay Colony") and [Plymouth Colony](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Plymouth_Colony "Plymouth Colony") started to collect these records in a central location, but the practice died out by the mid-17th Century. The only vital records closed to the public are the original births of amended records and those can be opened by a judge.

The locality-guide agent has completed and saved the guide as **loc_001** in the project. Here's a summary of what it produced:

---

**Jalisco, Mexico — Locality Research Guide (1880–1920)**

**Civil Registration**
- Civil registers were kept by each **municipio** (municipality), not at the state level — your search must start from the specific town where events occurred.
- **FamilySearch** has a free, indexed and imaged collection for Jalisco civil registration (births, marriages, deaths).
- **Ancestry** holds the same Jalisco records behind a subscription.

**Catholic Parish Registers**
- These matter significantly because they cover events before full civil enforcement (post-1867) and run *alongside* civil marriages well into the 1900s.

**Two-Surname Families**
- Search the **paternal surname alone** as a separate strategy.
- Women retain their **maiden names** in these records — don't search only under a married name.

**Other Record Types**
- Divorce papers are held by **municipio courts**, separate from the civil registers.

**Next Steps**
- Use the **research-plan** agent to convert this guide into a sequenced search plan.
- The agent flagged a note: the project's stated objective appeared to reference a Pennsylvania ancestor — you may want to confirm that this Mexico work belongs in this project (or start a dedicated project for it).

# Jalisco, Mexico Genealogy



[Mexico](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Genealogy "Mexico Genealogy")

State of Jalisco

Guide to **State of Jalisco ancestry, family history and genealogy:** birth records, marriage records, death records, census records, parish registers, and military records.

## History

Jalisco is located in western Mexico and is bordered by six states, Nayarit, Zacatecas, Aguascalientes, Guanajuato, Michoacán, and Colima. Jalisco became the 9th state of Mexico in Dec 23, 1823 and Guadalajara is the capital. The state is home to two significant indigenous populations, the Huichols and the Nahuas.[[1]](#cite_note-1)
