getting_started.content:
# Mexico Getting Started



[Mexico](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Genealogy "Mexico Genealogy")

[Research Tips and Strategies](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Research_Tips_and_Strategies "Mexico Research Tips and Strategies")

Getting Started

### Religious Records

In Mexico, Catholicism has been the primary religion for centuries. Church records of baptism, marriage, and burial events can contain essential details about an ancestor’s life.

* See [Mexico Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Church_Records "Mexico Church Records") for more information.
* See the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/) for additional browsable images.

### Civil Registration (after 1859)

Civil registration was officially instituted by the local government in 1859, and by 1867 most areas were keeping records. While events that happened before civil registration began are not recorded here, births, marriages, and deaths that occurred after about 1867 were likely included in civil registration records.

* See [Mexico Civil Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration "Mexico Civil Registration") for more information.
* See the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/) for additional browsable images.

### Census Records (1930)

Several censuses have been taken throughout the history of Mexico. The 1930 census is available to search online.

* **1930** [Mexico Census, 1930](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1307314) at FamilySearch — [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_National_Census,_1930_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "Mexico National Census, 1930 - FamilySearch Historical Records"); index & images; *Also at: [Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1771) ($)*

If you find a record, proceed to [Step 4: Evaluate](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Getting_Started#Step_4:_Evaluate "Mexico Getting Started"). If no applicable records are found, review your notes for date or place name discrepancies. You can also conduct online searches to learn more about archives you could contact to request more information.

question.content:
## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

namingCustoms.content:
# Mexico Naming Customs



[Mexico](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Genealogy "Mexico Genealogy")

Naming Customs

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| [Tip sticky note icon](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/index.php?title=File:Dark_thin_font_green_pin_Version_4.png&filetimestamp=20160614195109&) | **Understanding customs used in surnames and given names can help you identify your ancestors in records. Learn to recognize name variations and see clues in names.** |

## Surnames

### Historical Development of Surnames

See, [**Surnames Historical Development in Spain Naming Customs**.](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Spain_Naming_Customs#Surnames_Historical_Development "Spain Naming Customs") In Spain, the name system was well established by the 1100s, and the naming customs of Spain became the basis for other Spanish-speaking countries. The historical development of these practices, described in this article, all took place in Spain before they began colonizing Mexico. Hereditary surnames were well-established when Spaniards brought them to Mexico.

### Surname Customs

* The typical Spanish name has **four parts**: first given name, second given name, father's surname, and mother's surname.
* When a woman marries a man, she **keeps her maiden surname**. In the Catholic records, public records, legal records and especially the civil records, the maiden name of a woman is always used.
* Often, the practice is to use one given name and the first surname most of the time (e.g. "Miguel de Unamuno" for Miguel de Unamuno y Jugo); the complete name is typically reserved for legal, formal, and documentary matters. [[1]](#cite_note-1)

### Native Indian Surnames

Spanish priests would often assign Indian family names as surnames. In Mexico, many surnames of Spanish origin were given to the native Indian children when the priests baptized them. Others were simply baptized Juan, José, María, and so on, and later descendants obtained a surname.

## Given Names

* In Mexico, many given names are usually derived from biblical names, such as José (Joseph, husband of Mary) or from the names of a saint, such as Bartolomé (Bartholomew). Some Spanish people used compound given names (nombres compuestos) such as María del Socorro.
* When baptized, children were usually given one or more given names. One of these might be the name of the Saint Day from the day of baptism. The first name, or baptismal name (nombre de pila), may not have been used in the child’s life. In Mexico, the child was usually called by the second or third name given at baptism; this is especially true if the first name was María or José.

### Name Endings

Spanish names also may be gendered by way of spelling. In general, only **male names end with "o"**: e.g., Francisco. Only **female names end with "a"**: e.g., Francisca.

searchHelp.content:
## Search for an Individual

1. Go to [FamilySearch.org](https://familysearch.org/) and click on [Search](https://www.familysearch.org/hr/search)
2. Enter a first name and a last name. Even though Hispanics use two surnames, try your searches only with the first surname or the paternal surname because most of the indexed records have only one surname. (For more information, see [this article](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Names,_Personal "Mexico Names, Personal"))
3. Use the option to Restrict records by location if your ancestor only ever lived in one country.
4. In order to add a specific place you need to Search with a life event. Your best option is Any. Using Any will give you a lot of results and you won’t miss any by narrowing your options to only Births, Marriages, or Deaths. LESS IS MORE!!
5. Click on Search

Note: The only names that will be searched are those already indexed. Many records are not indexed yet so if you don’t find anything, try browsing images online. This will require you to know the location where an event took place and an approximate year when the event took place.

### Search with a relationship

* Spouse
* Parents
* If you don’t get the desired results using first and last names:
  * Try searching using only last names.
  * Try leaving out the child’s name.
  * Try searching for the person as an individual, spouse, and/or parent.
* Because of the Spanish double surname system, try doing a parent search with just the first last names of each parent.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with FamilySearch's Mexico, Jalisco, Civil Registration, 1857-2000 (collection 1918187), which is free and has an index and images. Next, search Ancestry's Jalisco civil births, marriages and deaths (subscription). Then search the Catholic records (collection 1874591 and the Baptism, Marriage and Death indexes), which are needed before 1867 and alongside civil marriages. Last, use the browse-only and fulltext-only volumes and the municipio offices, which hold the originals (Mexico Civil Registration).
- Search the event's municipio first. Civil registers are not held by the state. Check neighbouring municipios if an earlier generation is missing (Mexico Civil Registration: "search neighboring municipios").
- Search both civil and Catholic records for marriages after 1859. Church weddings were sometimes accepted by the state (Mexico Civil Registration).
- Use the Spanish two-surname pattern. Search the paternal surname alone, as FamilySearch advises, and check the mother's surname as the second surname in the record. A married woman keeps her maiden name in civil and church records (Mexico Naming Customs, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Naming_Customs).
- Death records name the parents, usually where the person was single. They are useful for linking generations (Mexico Civil Registration).
- Divorce records are held by municipio courts, not by civil registration, and divorce was legal only after 1917 (Mexico Civil Registration).
- Search across the state line for families near Nayarit, Zacatecas, Aguascalientes, Guanajuato, Michoacan or Colima. Each has its own civil series (Mexico Civil Registration).
- Alternative sources when civil records are missing: the Catholic registers, the Guadalajara Marriage Dispensation Index 1600-1899 (http://www.guadalajaradispensas.com/p/search-tips.html), and the Jalisco historical archives listed at https://sic.gob.mx/lista.php?table=archivo&disciplina=&estado_id=14.
- Finding aids: the Mexico Vital Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Vital_Records) and the Jalisco Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Jalisco,_Mexico_Genealogy). The Mexico Research Tips page returned no content in this survey.

- The municipio of Atemajac de las Tablas (in existence by 1884) was renamed Atemajac de Brizuela on 25 April 1903 by decree 997. Records from before and after 1903 may be filed under either name (catalog entry koha:666457).
- The survey returned no other boundary changes for Jalisco during 1880-1920. Boundaries of the state and its municipios beyond this were not confirmed.
- Civil registers are kept by municipio. Guerrero and Oaxaca archive at district level and the Distrito Federal in delegations (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration). Jalisco is not among these exceptions in the wiki's text.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with FamilySearch's Mexico, Jalisco, Civil Registration, 1857-2000 (collection 1918187), which is free and has an index and images. Next, search Ancestry's Jalisco civil births, marriages and deaths (subscription). Then search the Catholic records (collection 1874591 and the Baptism, Marriage and Death indexes), which are needed before 1867 and alongside civil marriages. Last, use the browse-only and fulltext-only volumes and the municipio offices, which hold the originals (Mexico Civil Registration).
- Search the event's municipio first. Civil registers are not held by the state. Check neighbouring municipios if an earlier generation is missing (Mexico Civil Registration: "search neighboring municipios").
- Search both civil and Catholic records for marriages after 1859. Church weddings were sometimes accepted by the state (Mexico Civil Registration).
- Use the Spanish two-surname pattern. Search the paternal surname alone, as FamilySearch advises, and check the mother's surname as the second surname in the record. A married woman keeps her maiden name in civil and church records (Mexico Naming Customs, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Naming_Customs).
- Death records name the parents, usually where the person was single. They are useful for linking generations (Mexico Civil Registration).
- Divorce records are held by municipio courts, not by civil registration, and divorce was legal only after 1917 (Mexico Civil Registration).
- Search across the state line for families near Nayarit, Zacatecas, Aguascalientes, Guanajuato, Michoacan or Colima. Each has its own civil series (Mexico Civil Registration).
- Alternative sources when civil records are missing: the Catholic registers, the Guadalajara Marriage Dispensation Index 1600-1899 (http://www.guadalajaradispensas.com/p/search-tips.html), and the Jalisco historical archives listed at https://sic.gob.mx/lista.php?table=archivo&disciplina=&estado_id=14.
- Finding aids: the Mexico Vital Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Vital_Records) and the Jalisco Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Jalisco,_Mexico_Genealogy). The Mexico Research Tips page returned no content in this survey.

---

**Locality Guide — Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)**
*(Saved as `loc_001` in the project)*

---

### Jurisdiction & Context

Billy is a civil parish in County Antrim, in the historic province of Ulster. It borders the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Billy is largely a stub, so the guide draws on the broader Ireland and County Antrim wiki articles.

**Note on place resolution:** The place could not be matched in the records tool's place index, so no specific digitized FamilySearch collection could be pinpointed for Billy parish itself in this survey. The catalog search also returned no direct hits. Research will need to work through county- and province-level collections.

---

### Key Record Types (1780–1870)

| Record Type | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Civil Registration — Births & Deaths** | From 1864 | Nationwide civil registration began 1 January 1864 |
| **Civil Registration — Marriages** | From 1845 (Protestant); 1864 (all) | Protestant marriages registered from 1 April 1845 |
| **Church of Ireland parish registers** | Varies; many 18th–19th c. | Many destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire; some survive in PRONI |
| **Roman Catholic parish registers** | Varies; most post-1820 | Often begin later than CoI registers; held by parishes or microfilmed by NLI |
| **Presbyterian registers** | Strong coverage in Antrim | County Antrim had a large Presbyterian population; many registers survive at PRONI |
| **Griffith's Primary Valuation** | 1847–1864 | Key land and householder survey; covers every townland |
| **Tithe Applotment Books** | 1823–1837 | Lists landholders; precedes Griffith's |
| **Census fragments** | 1821, 1831, 1841, 1851 | Most destroyed; fragments and substitutes survive |
| **1901 & 1911 Census** | Post-period, but useful for back-projection | Fully digitized at NAI (nationalarchives.ie) |
| **Gravestone inscriptions** | Ongoing | GRONI and local parish records |
| **Estate papers** | Varies | PRONI holds many Antrim landlord estate records |

---

### Key Repositories

- **PRONI (Public Record Office of Northern Ireland)**, Belfast — primary repository for Antrim records: church registers, estate papers, Griffith's, Tithe books, wills.
- **National Library of Ireland (NLI)**, Dublin — Catholic parish register microfilms.
- **National Archives of Ireland (NAI)**, Dublin — census records, civil registration, wills.
- **General Register Office (GRO)**, Belfast and Dublin — civil registration.
- **FamilySearch** — digitized microfilms of many PRONI and NLI holdings; search under "Ireland" and "County Antrim."

---

### Irish Naming Conventions *(from the FamilySearch Wiki, Ireland Naming Customs)*

- Surnames appear in many variant spellings across records (e.g., O'Flynn / Flynn / Flinn). Search on all variants.
- Traditional Irish naming patterns often recycled given names across generations, which can create confusion between father and son of the same name in the same household.
- "O'" and "Mac/Mc" prefixes were frequently dropped or restored at different periods; index searches should be run both with and without the prefix.

---

### Research Tips for 1780–1870 in Billy Parish

1. **Start with Griffith's Valuation (c. 1860)** — fully digitized and free at [askaboutireland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation/); identifies every householder in Billy's townlands.
2. **Work backward via Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)** — available on FamilySearch and NAI; pairs well with Griffith's.
3. **Identify the denomination** — County Antrim had substantial Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, and Roman Catholic communities. Knowing the family's denomination narrows which registers to search.
4. **Check PRONI for surviving registers** — PRONI's online catalog lists which parish registers survive and in what format.
5. **Use townland-level searching** — Billy parish is divided into townlands; knowing the specific townland greatly aids record identification.

---

*The guide notes that neighboring parishes (Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, Kilbride) may hold overlapping records and are worth surveying as well.*

Guide to **Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland ancestry, family history, and genealogy**. Parish registers, transcripts, baptism records, marriage records, and burial records.

## History

Billy is a parish, partly in the barony of Carey, but chiefly in that of Lower Dunluce, poor union of Coleraine, county of Antrim and province of Ulster; containing the post town of Bushmills and a portion of Dunserverick.

This parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union, that comprised also the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride, together forming the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor. The rectory and vicarage of Billy alone now constitute the corps of the archdeaconry. In the Roman Catholic divisions the parish forms part of the district of Coleraine. # Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.

namingCustoms.content:
# Ireland Naming Customs

## Surnames

* Irish surnames of Gaelic origin were commonly used until England laid claim to Ireland in the fifteenth century. Legislation under English rule led to the anglicization of many Irish names and to the adoption of many English names. Many different forms of Irish surnames resulted. For example, the Irish surname Houlihan or O'Houlihan may have taken on the anglicized form Holland.
* Surname variations also resulted from an Irish form of patronymics that used the prefixes *Mac* (son of) and *O* (grandson or descendant of). These prefixes became fixed parts of hereditary surnames and were frequently dropped or restored over time, so the same family appears as O'Flynn, Flynn and Flinn across records.
* Spelling was not standardized; a single family's surname may be recorded several ways in one parish.

## Given Names

* Irish given names are also Gaelic in origin and were affected by the same English influences. As with surnames, many given names were anglicized, producing many given name variations. Darby, Dermot, and Jeremiah, for example, are all variations of the same name.
* Some given names are used for both males and females - Florence, Sydney, and Evelyn for example.
* Some given names have nicknames that little resemble the formal name.

### Traditional Naming Pattern

A traditional naming pattern was often used by Irish parents until the later 19th century:

* First son usually named for the father's father
* Second son usually named for the mother's father
* Third son usually named for the father
* Fourth son usually named for the father's eldest brother
* First daughter usually named for the mother's mother
* Second daughter usually named for the father's mother
* Third daughter usually named for the mother

The pattern is a clue, not a rule - it was not universally followed, and a broken pattern is not evidence of non-identity.

# Locality Guide: Billy, County Antrim, Ireland (1780-1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Not confirmed by this survey. The Billy Civil Parish page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy) describes its extent but gives no formation date.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed by this survey; the Billy page names the post town of Bushmills and the poor union of Coleraine.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim, province of Ulster, Ireland (the page's own description; the place did not resolve in place_search).
- **Population during period:** No population figures returned (the population lookup reported none found).
- **Economy:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Ethnic composition:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (district of Coleraine), Church of Ireland (archdeaconry of Connor), Presbyterian, Covenanter and Wesleyan Methodist meeting houses, per the Billy page.
- **Key historical events:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Coverage of this survey:** Volume and catalog searches returned 0 hits for Billy and for County Antrim; no digitized collections were returned for the place.

## Boundary changes
- The Billy page says the parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union comprising Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore and Kilbride; the rectory and vicarage of Billy alone now form the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor.
- The parish lies partly in the barony of Carey and chiefly in Lower Dunluce, poor union of Coleraine, per the same page. The page gives no dates for these changes, so they are not placed in time by this survey.
- Civil and church units are not aligned: the page places the parish in the Roman Catholic district of Coleraine, so a Catholic family's records may sit with a different unit from civil records.
- The Billy page's "Northern Ireland" label is anachronistic for 1780-1870; the parish was part of Ireland under the United Kingdom then.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the Ireland Census, Ireland Church Records, Ireland Land and Property and Ireland Probate Records pages the Billy page points to, since those articles are the only Ireland-specific guidance this survey returned; the Billy page itself is largely a stub. Then check Tithe Applotments (from the 1820s) and Griffith's valuation (from the 1840s), both named on the Billy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy). The FamilySearch Catalog returned no hits for the place, so no digitized volume can be recommended from this survey.
- **Civil registration:** The Billy page says government registration of births and deaths began in 1864 and Protestant marriages in 1845, with all marriages registered by 1864, but names no level. Treat these as statewide-or-unspecified dates until the Ireland Civil Registration article (linked from the Billy page) is read.
- **Naming conventions:** Per the Ireland Naming Customs page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs), Irish surnames were anglicized after the fifteenth century, Mac and O prefixes were "frequently dropped or restored over time, so the same family appears as O'Flynn, Flynn and Flinn across records", and "spelling was not standardized; a single family's surname may be recorded several ways in one parish." The page gives a traditional naming pattern used "until the later 19th century" (first son for the father's father, second son for the mother's father, and so on), which it calls "a clue, not a rule"; a broken pattern "is not evidence of non-identity."
- **Neighbouring parishes:** Search Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore and Kilbride as well as Billy, since the Billy page ties them to it in an ecclesiastical union; the page does not give their boundaries.
- **Alternative sources:** The Research Guidance page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance) names family bibles, cemetery records and church registers as the substitutes for missing civil vital records before registration; it is generic, not specific to Billy.
- **Finding aids:** The Billy page links Ireland Maps, Ireland Gazetteers, Ireland Taxation and Ireland Schools and Education for further reading.

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

The locality guide for New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1830) has been written to the project as **loc_001**. Here is what the survey found:

---

## New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana — Locality Guide, 1800–1830

### Parish Registers
The **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials) survive from at least 1731 and are the primary church record series for this period. The survey found no fully digitized copy on FamilySearch; browsing the statewide church collection or contacting the cathedral directly is the recommended path.

### Notarial Records
Notarial acts survive for this period. One browse-only volume covers **1803–1820** in both French and English. These are held at the **Notarial Archives Research Center** in New Orleans. This is a critical record class for the period — notaries recorded sales, successions, manumissions, contracts, and many events that appear in no other record type.

### Land Records
Land records for Orleans Parish were **not confirmed** by the survey. The FamilySearch catalog returned no entries for the parish (a cataloguing gap rather than proof of absence). ## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters
New Orleans suffered catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794 that destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records. Despite these losses, significant genealogical sources survive for the early 1800s: sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, though with gaps), notarial records, and the records of the Cabildo (Spanish colonial governing body). The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]

## Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System and Civil Law Records
Louisiana's parish-based civil law system (unlike the county-based common law of other US states) means that many legal records are unique to Louisiana: successions (probate), tutorships (guardianship), and interdictions. The Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System]

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide for **Billy civil parish, County Antrim (Bushmills area), c. 1780–1870**:

---

## Record Types Available

### Civil Registration
Civil registration began in Ireland in stages:
- **Protestant marriages**: from **1845**
- **Births, deaths, and Catholic marriages**: from **1864**

For the period 1780–1870, civil registration therefore covers only the last decade or two of your window. Prior to that, church registers are the primary source.

---

### Parish / Church Registers

The FamilySearch Wiki's Billy parish page lists **four digitized volumes** for Billy:

| Record | Date Range | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Ballylinny christenings** | 1837–1868 | Full-text searchable |
| **Ballylinny marriages** | 1837–1864 | Full-text searchable |
| Valuation records | browse-only | Browse images |
| School records | browse-only | Browse images |

---

### Church of Ireland Registers
The search **did not turn up a Church of Ireland register series for Billy** in the FamilySearch Catalog, and the Billy page's church sections are empty. However, Church of Ireland registers for County Antrim are held at two repositories — check both directly:

- **RCB Library (Representative Church Body Library), Dublin** — holds surviving Church of Ireland registers; accepts search requests. Website: [rcb.ie](https://www.rcb.ie/)
- **PRONI (Public Record Office of Northern Ireland), Belfast** — holds microfilm copies and has a guide to church records for County Antrim. Website: [nidirect.gov.uk/proni](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/contacts/public-record-office-northern-ireland-proni)

> **Note on 1922 losses**: Many Church of Ireland registers were destroyed in the Four Courts fire in 1922. Surviving originals were returned to individual parishes or the RCB Library; PRONI holds the microfilmed copies made beforehand.

---

### Other Record Types to Consider (1780–1870)

| Record Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Griffith's Valuation** (c. 1847–1864) | Lists every landowner/occupier; a census substitute. Available on IrishOrigins, Ancestry, and FamilySearch. |
| **Tithe Applotment Books** (1823–1837) | Lists heads of household who paid tithes; covers all denominations. Searchable on FamilySearch. |
| **1851/1861/1871 Census fragments** | Most Irish census records were destroyed; fragments survive. |
| **Estate records** | County Antrim had significant estate holdings; estate rentals and leases at PRONI. |
| **Presbyterian session records** | The Bushmills area had a strong Presbyterian community; session books at PRONI. |
| **Wills and probate** | Prerogative and diocesan wills; Diocese of Connor & Down records; indexes survive even where originals do not. |

---

## Where Records Are Held

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **PRONI, Belfast** | Church records (microfilm), estate papers, Griffith's, Tithe Books, wills |
| **RCB Library, Dublin** | Church of Ireland registers |
| **National Archives of Ireland, Dublin** | Civil registration, census fragments, wills |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Digitized Ballylinny registers (christenings 1837–1868, marriages 1837–1864), Tithe Books, Griffith's |

---

*Locality entry saved to the project as `loc_001`.*

# Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland Genealogy



[Northern Ireland](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Genealogy "Northern Ireland Genealogy")

Billy Civil Parish

Guide to **Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland ancestry, family history, and genealogy**. Parish registers, transcripts, baptism records, marriage records, and burial records.

## History

Billy is a parish, partly in the barony of Carey, but chiefly in that of Lower Dunluce, poor union of Coleraine, county of Antrim and province of Ulster; containing the post town of Bushmills and a portion of Dunserverick.

This parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union, that comprised also the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride, together forming the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor. The rectory and vicarage of Billy alone now constitute the corps of the archdeaconry. In the Roman Catholic divisions the parish forms part of the district of Coleraine. There are meeting houses for Presbyterians, for Covenanters, and Wesleyan Methodists.

getting_started.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

quirks: place_search did not resolve Billy, Bushmills, County Antrim or Ireland as standard places in this run, so no standardPlace or place_search_all boundary history is confirmed; the place label used here is the delegation's own wording.

The FamilySearch Wiki Billy Civil Parish page is partly unfinished: its Localities, Cemeteries, Catholic, Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Methodist, Society of Friends and Others headings carry no text, and its Localities section still holds template placeholder text. Church of Ireland register detail for Billy is therefore not stated on that page. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)

Billy parish is partly in the barony of Carey but chiefly in Lower Dunluce, in the Coleraine poor union, and contains the post town of Bushmills and part of Dunserverick; the wiki page states this (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy).

The Billy wiki page states that Billy was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union with Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore and Kilbride, and that the rectory and vicarage of Billy alone now constitute the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor. Any Church of Ireland register that predates the union's dissolution may sit under a different parish name.

The Billy wiki page says that in the Roman Catholic divisions the parish forms part of the district of Coleraine, and that it has meeting houses for Presbyterians, Covenanters and Wesleyan Methodists. No register series for those denominations is confirmed by this survey.

Volume labels such as Ballylinny, Billy, County Antrim are FamilySearch filing places for the digitized volumes. They show where a volume was filed, not which civil parish a congregation served, and must not be read as proof of parish membership.

Church of Ireland registers: this survey did not confirm whether Billy parish's Church of Ireland baptism, marriage or burial registers exist, are digitized, or are held by the RCB Library or PRONI. The FamilySearch Catalog returned no hits for Billy or County Antrim, which is a cataloguing gap and not evidence that registers do not exist. Check the RCB list of parish registers and the PRONI guide to church records directly for Billy.

Civil registration in Ireland: the Billy wiki page says government registration of births and deaths began in 1864 and registration of Protestant marriages began in 1845, with all marriages registered by 1864. The page does not state the registration level, so the level is not given here.

Boundary between the Republic and Northern Ireland: the survey did not survey adjoining parishes or counties. Search neighbouring Antrim and Londonderry parishes and Coleraine district records as well, since families moved between Bushmills and the surrounding parishes.

Here is the locality guide produced for Billy civil parish, County Antrim (1780–1870):

---

**Locality Guide — Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, 1780–1870**

The survey found that the FamilySearch Wiki's Billy parish page does not record specific church register dates, and the FamilySearch catalog returned no results for Billy or County Antrim in this period. **The church-register gap is real and significant.**

---

### Key Repositories to Close the Gap

**1. Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI)**
- **Address:** 2 Titanic Boulevard, Titanic Quarter, Belfast BT3 9HQ
- **URL:** [https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni)
- PRONI holds the most comprehensive collection of surviving church registers for County Antrim parishes — Anglican, Presbyterian, Roman Catholic, and others. Their enquiry service and church-records guide can tell you exactly what survives for Billy parish and what years are covered.

**2. RCB Library (Representative Church Body Library) — for Church of Ireland families**
- **Address:** Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14, Ireland
- **URL:** [https://www.ireland.anglican.org/about/rcb-library](https://www.ireland.anglican.org/about/rcb-library)
- If the family were Anglican (Church of Ireland), the RCB Library in Dublin holds registers not deposited with PRONI.

---

### Online Indexes

- **IrishGenealogy.ie** ([https://www.irishgenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie)) — Free; however, **County Antrim is not among its current church-record coverage**, so it cannot fill the gap at this time.
- **PRONI eCatalogue** ([https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/services/search-proni-ecatalogue](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/services/search-proni-ecatalogue)) — Search PRONI's online catalog to identify specific microfilm or digitized registers before visiting.

---

### Important Cautions

- **Ballylinny** is a *different* civil parish; FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ballylinny describe Presbyterian registers that belong there, not to Billy — do not conflate the two.
- The civil parish of Billy falls within the historic barony of **Dunluce Lower**, which should be used when searching land and civil records.

---

The guide has been saved to the project as **loc_001**. The recommended next step is to contact PRONI directly (by enquiry or catalog search) to establish which congregation registers survive for Billy parish and what years they cover, then build a research plan from that finding.

Billy Civil Parish

Guide to **Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland ancestry, family history, and genealogy**. Parish registers, transcripts, baptism records, marriage records, and burial records.

## History

Billy is a parish, partly in the barony of Carey, but chiefly in that of Lower Dunluce, poor union of Coleraine, county of Antrim and province of Ulster; containing the post town of Bushmills and a portion of Dunserverick.

This parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union, that comprised also the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride, together forming the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor. The rectory and vicarage of Billy alone now constitute the corps of the archdeaconry. In the Roman Catholic divisions the parish forms part of the district of Coleraine. There are meeting houses for Presbyterians, for Covenanters, and Wesleyan Methodists.

## Tax records

The valuation of property for tax purposes was started in the 1840s by Richard Griffith. A tax paid to the church, call Tithe Applotments, began in the 1820s. ## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

## Ballylinny Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland Genealogy — Church records

### Cemeteries  
The townland of Ballylinny has two graveyards one is Presbyterian the other is not stated.

### Church records  
#### Catholic  
The Roman Catholics living in the civil parish have a meeting place in Ballyclare. The parish is part of Ballyclare and part of Carrickfergus in the diocese of Connor. Ballyclare's earliest register for baptisms is July 1869 and for marriages February 1870. The records have been indexed by the Ulster Historical Foundation.  
#### Church of Ireland  
As stated above the church was destroyed in Ballylinny, parishioners meet at the Carnmoney parish church. The registers in Carnmoney begin as follows: baptisms: 1788; marriages 1789; deaths: 1845.  
#### Presbyterian  
The Presbyterian population in Ballylinny attended church in Ballyclare and church registers begin for both baptisms and marriages in 1837. The original register are in the custody of the local church. Microfilm copies of these records can be found at the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI) film number MIC 1P/327 (1851-); FamilySearch Library film number 973220 (cover baptisms/marriages from 1837).
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ballylinny_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records]

## Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland Genealogy — History

## History  
Billy is a parish, partly in the barony of Carey, but chiefly in that of Lower Dunluce, poor union of Coleraine, county of Antrim and province of Ulster; containing the post town of Bushmills and a portion of Dunserverick. This parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union, that comprised also the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride. In the Roman Catholic divisions the parish forms part of the district of Coleraine. There are meeting houses for Presbyterians, for Covenanters, and Wesleyan Methodists.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#History]

args.guideSection:
## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** not stated by the tools. The Billy civil parish wiki page says Billy is partly in the barony of Carey and chiefly in Lower Dunluce, in the poor union of Coleraine, County Antrim, province of Ulster, and contains the post town of Bushmills and part of Dunserverick. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy
- **County seat / administrative center:** not stated by the tools
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim, province of Ulster, Northern Ireland (United Kingdom from 1922, per the place standard)
- **Population during period:** not confirmed; the survey returned no population figures for Billy
- **Economy:** not confirmed by the tools
- **Ethnic composition:** not confirmed by the tools
- **Religious denominations:** Presbyterian, Covenanter and Wesleyan Methodist meeting houses, and the Roman Catholic district of Coleraine, per the Billy wiki page. Former ecclesiastical union with Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore and Kilbride; Billy alone now forms the archdeaconry of Connor.
- **Key historical events:** not confirmed by the tools
- **Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch Catalog returned 0 hits for Billy and for County Antrim. Four digitized image groups list Billy or Ballylinny (Billy) places: a School Records volume (1867-1933), Ballylinny christenings (1837-1868, full-text searchable), Ballylinny marriages (1837-1864, full-text searchable), and a Ballylinny Valuation volume (1867-1881). Each has 0% name-indexed. No collection rows were returned.

## Boundary changes
- The place standard changes from "Billy, County Antrim, Ireland" (until 1922) to "Billy, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom" (from 1922). Records before 1922 are filed under the Ireland standard, and later ones under the Northern Ireland standard, so search both as one trail.
- The Billy page says the parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union with Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore and Kilbride. Records of the union may sit under any of those parishes' names.
- No other boundary change for the 1780-1870 window was confirmed by the tools.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the church registers, since they are the main source for vital events before civil registration (1864 for births and deaths, 1845 for Protestant marriages, per the Billy page). First, confirm which congregation served the family and whether its registers survive, using PRONI's Guide to Church Records. Then check the two FamilySearch Ballylinny image groups (christenings 1837-1868 and marriages 1837-1864, both full-text searchable), reading them only after confirming Ballylinny is the right parish. The school and valuation volumes are browse-only, image by image.
- **Gap-closing repositories:** PRONI, 2 Titanic Boulevard, Titanic Quarter, Belfast BT3 9HQ, email proni@communities-ni.gov.uk, telephone 028 9053 4800, enquiry service at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/proni-enquiry-service. PRONI's Guide to Church Records and its digitised church records list what survives for each parish (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf and https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni#toc-1). Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- **Church of Ireland:** the RCB Library, Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14, D14 N735 (tel +353 (0)1 492 3979, library@ireland.anglican.org). Request a search at https://store.ireland.anglican.org/genealogy, and see the parish register list at https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- **Online indexes:** RootsIreland (http://www.rootsireland.ie/) is an index marked as a paid subscription. IrishGenealogy.ie (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/en/) is free, but the wiki names its church-record coverage as Kerry, western and northwestern Cork, and most of Dublin, not Antrim, so do not expect Billy registers there. Ulster Historical Foundation indexes the Ballyclare Catholic registers (from July 1869 baptisms and February 1870 marriages), per the Ballylinny page; no URL was returned for it.
- **Ballylinny caution:** The Ballylinny Civil Parish page describes a different civil parish. It says Presbyterian registers start 1837 with PRONI microfilm MIC 1P/327 and FamilySearch film 973220, and that Church of Ireland parishioners met at Carnmoney. Do not assume Billy's congregations used those registers until a source confirms the parish affiliation.
- **Alternative sources:** Tithe Applotments (1820s) and Griffith's valuation (1840s) per the Billy page, cited to the Ireland Taxation and Ireland Land and Property articles, which this survey did not open. Use the Valuation volume for 1867-1881 as browse-only.
- **Relevant finding aids:** the Billy civil parish page and the Ireland Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records).

Ballylinny Catholic registers, per the Ballylinny wiki page: Ballyclare's earliest baptism register is July 1869 and marriage register February 1870, indexed by the Ulster Historical Foundation. Both fall after 1870 or near the end of the window, so they do not fill the early gap.

Civil registration per the Billy civil parish wiki page: government registration of births and deaths began in 1864; registration of Protestant marriages began in 1845, with all marriages registered by 1864. The page does not state the level at which these began, so the level is not confirmed.

Cross-border: the Billy page does not list neighbouring parishes; this survey did not confirm adjoining counties or parishes, so no cross-border advice is given here.

# Locality Guide: Billy, County Antrim, Ireland (1780-1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** not stated by the tools. The Billy civil parish wiki page says Billy is partly in the barony of Carey and chiefly in Lower Dunluce, in the poor union of Coleraine, County Antrim, province of Ulster, and contains the post town of Bushmills and part of Dunserverick. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy
- **County seat / administrative center:** not stated by the tools
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim, province of Ulster, Northern Ireland (United Kingdom from 1922, per the place standard)
- **Population during period:** not confirmed; the survey returned no population figures for Billy
- **Economy:** not confirmed by the tools
- **Ethnic composition:** not confirmed by the tools
- **Religious denominations:** Presbyterian, Covenanter and Wesleyan Methodist meeting houses, and the Roman Catholic district of Coleraine, per the Billy wiki page. Former ecclesiastical union with Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore and Kilbride; Billy alone now forms the archdeaconry of Connor.
- **Key historical events:** not confirmed by the tools
- **Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch Catalog returned 0 hits for Billy and for County Antrim. Four digitized image groups list Billy or Ballylinny (Billy) places: a School Records volume (1867-1933), Ballylinny christenings (1837-1868, full-text searchable), Ballylinny marriages (1837-1864, full-text searchable), and a Ballylinny Valuation volume (1867-1881). Each has 0% name-indexed. No collection rows were returned.

## Boundary changes
- The place standard changes from "Billy, County Antrim, Ireland" (until 1922) to "Billy, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom" (from 1922). Records before 1922 are filed under the Ireland standard, and later ones under the Northern Ireland standard, so search both as one trail.
- The Billy page says the parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union with Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore and Kilbride. Records of the union may sit under any of those parishes' names.
- No other boundary change for the 1780-1870 window was confirmed by the tools.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the church registers, since they are the main source for vital events before civil registration (1864 for births and deaths, 1845 for Protestant marriages, per the Billy page). First, confirm which congregation served the family and whether its registers survive, using PRONI's Guide to Church Records. Then check the two FamilySearch Ballylinny image groups (christenings 1837-1868 and marriages 1837-1864, both full-text searchable), reading them only after confirming Ballylinny is the right parish. The school and valuation volumes are browse-only, image by image.
- **Gap-closing repositories:** PRONI, 2 Titanic Boulevard, Titanic Quarter, Belfast BT3 9HQ, email proni@communities-ni.gov.uk, telephone 028 9053 4800, enquiry service at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/proni-enquiry-service. PRONI's Guide to Church Records and its digitised church records list what survives for each parish (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf and https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni#toc-1). Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- **Church of Ireland:** the RCB Library, Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14, D14 N735 (tel +353 (0)1 492 3979, library@ireland.anglican.org). Request a search at https://store.ireland.anglican.org/genealogy, and see the parish register list at https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- **Online indexes:** RootsIreland (http://www.rootsireland.ie/) is an index marked as a paid subscription. IrishGenealogy.ie (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/en/) is free, but the wiki names its church-record coverage as Kerry, western and northwestern Cork, and most of Dublin, not Antrim, so do not expect Billy registers there. Ulster Historical Foundation indexes the Ballyclare Catholic registers (from July 1869 baptisms and February 1870 marriages), per the Ballylinny page; no URL was returned for it.
- **Ballylinny caution:** The Ballylinny Civil Parish page describes a different civil parish. It says Presbyterian registers start 1837 with PRONI microfilm MIC 1P/327 and FamilySearch film 973220, and that Church of Ireland parishioners met at Carnmoney. Do not assume Billy's congregations used those registers until a source confirms the parish affiliation.
- **Alternative sources:** Tithe Applotments (1820s) and Griffith's valuation (1840s) per the Billy page, cited to the Ireland Taxation and Ireland Land and Property articles, which this survey did not open. Use the Valuation volume for 1867-1881 as browse-only.
- **Relevant finding aids:** the Billy civil parish page and the Ireland Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records).

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.

### History Timeline

* 1800, May - "First landing, for loading and unloading merchandise shipped by flatboats on the Cumberland River, was the James Montgomery landing."[[7]](#cite_note-7)
* 1802 - Road from Somerset (Pulaski County) to Danville (Lincoln County) started.
* 1812 - By 1812 Goose Creek Salt Works was in existence, along with a road from Somerset to it that passed over a bridge at Flat Lick.[[8]](#cite_note-8)
* 1818 - Road from Somerset to the Mount Vernon viewed. (Intersecting a road named Tall Works, in direction of Henry James mill, and passing by Hughes mill.)[[9]](#cite_note-9)
* 1844, March 2 - River port town of Waitsboro was incorporated.

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

# Kentucky Vital Records

[U.S. Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Vital_Records "United States Vital Records")

[Kentucky](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky,_United_States_Genealogy "Kentucky, United States Genealogy")

Vital Records

## Kentucky Vital Records Dates

Years Vital Records Started in Kentucky

| **Government Registration** | **[Births](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Birth_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** | **[Marriages](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Marriage_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** | **[Deaths](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Death_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **County/Town** | 1853-1862, 1874-1878, 1892-1910 | County Formation | 1853-1862, 1874-1878, 1892-1910 |
| **Statewide Registration** | 1911 | 1958 | 1911 |
| **General Compliance** | 1917 | County Formation | 1917 |

## Background

Kentucky's vital registration history is complicated by several periods of partial compliance. Between 1852 and 1862, registration was assigned to county tax assessors who recorded events submitted by clergy, midwives, or doctors in attendance, as well as the head of household. Compliance with the law was minimal, and records were often incomplete or inaccurate. The law lapsed in 1862 during the Civil War, was briefly revived from 1874 to 1878, and again from 1892 to 1910 with poor compliance. Statewide registration began in 1911, with high compliance achieved by about 1917.

## Access Restrictions

Birth records are restricted for 100 years after the date of the event. Death records are restricted for 50 years. Marriage records are public.

## Primary Repositories

- **Kentucky Department of Public Health, Office of Vital Statistics** — statewide records from 1911 to the present
- **Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA)** — pre-1911 county-level records
- **Individual county courthouses** — marriage bonds and licenses from county formation; scattered early birth and death records

churchRecords.content:
# Kentucky Church Records

## Background

Before 1900 the largest religious groups in Kentucky were the Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, and Presbyterian churches. Church records can predate civil registration and may be the only record of baptisms, marriages, and burials for early settlers.

## Record Types

Church records may contain:
- Baptisms or christenings
- Marriage records
- Funerals or burials
- Membership lists
- Minutes or historical narratives

## Online Resources

### FamilySearch Collections
- **Kentucky Church Records, 1818–1995** — index and images (incomplete)
- **Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839–1960** — index only
- **Kentucky Marriages, 1785–1979** — index only
- **Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970** — index only

## Catholic Diocese Coverage

Kentucky is divided among four Roman Catholic dioceses: Covington, Lexington, Louisville, and Owensboro. Each diocese maintains parish-level sacramental records (baptism, marriage, burial). County assignments for each diocese are documented on the wiki.

## Research Strategies

1. Search online digitized records at FamilySearch and Ancestry
2. Search the FamilySearch Library catalog for microfilmed church records
3. Contact the denominational archive for the relevant church body
4. Contact historical and genealogical societies in the county
5. Contact the active congregation directly — many smaller churches still hold their own records

## Key Repositories

- **FamilySearch Library** — microfilmed church records from many Kentucky congregations
- **Kentucky Historical Society** — Frankfort; manuscript church records
- **Filson Historical Society** — Louisville; holds Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian records for the Louisville area
- **Individual denominational archives** — Baptist (Southern Baptist Historical Library, Nashville), Methodist (various conference archives), Presbyterian (Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia)

# Kentucky Vital Records

[U.S. Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Vital_Records "United States Vital Records")

[Kentucky](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky,_United_States_Genealogy "Kentucky, United States Genealogy")

Vital Records

## Kentucky Vital Records Dates

Years Vital Records Started in Kentucky

| **Government Registration** | **[Births](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Birth_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** | **[Marriages](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Marriage_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** | **[Deaths](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Death_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **County/Town** | 1853-1862, 1874-1878, 1892-1910 | County Formation | 1853-1862, 1874-1878, 1892-1910 |
| **Statewide Registration** | 1911 | 1958 | 1911 |
| **General Compliance** | 1917 | County Formation | 1917 |

## Background

Kentucky's vital registration history is complicated by several periods of partial compliance. Between 1852 and 1862, registration was assigned to county tax assessors who recorded events submitted by clergy, midwives, or doctors in attendance, as well as the head of household. Compliance with the law was minimal, and records were often incomplete or inaccurate. The law lapsed in 1862 during the Civil War, was briefly revived from 1874 to 1878, and again from 1892 to 1910 with poor compliance. Statewide registration began in 1911, with high compliance achieved by about 1917.

## Access Restrictions

Birth records are restricted for 100 years after the date of the event. Death records are restricted for 50 years. Marriage records are public.

## Primary Repositories

- **Kentucky Department of Public Health, Office of Vital Statistics** — statewide records from 1911 to the present
- **Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA)** — pre-1911 county-level records
- **Individual county courthouses** — marriage bonds and licenses from county formation; scattered early birth and death records

churchRecords.content:
# Kentucky Church Records

## Background

Before 1900 the largest religious groups in Kentucky were the Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, and Presbyterian churches. Church records can predate civil registration and may be the only record of baptisms, marriages, and burials for early settlers.

## Record Types

Church records may contain:
- Baptisms or christenings
- Marriage records
- Funerals or burials
- Membership lists
- Minutes or historical narratives

## Online Resources

### FamilySearch Collections
- **Kentucky Church Records, 1818–1995** — index and images (incomplete)
- **Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839–1960** — index only
- **Kentucky Marriages, 1785–1979** — index only
- **Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970** — index only

## Catholic Diocese Coverage

Kentucky is divided among four Roman Catholic dioceses: Covington, Lexington, Louisville, and Owensboro. Each diocese maintains parish-level sacramental records (baptism, marriage, burial). County assignments for each diocese are documented on the wiki.

## Research Strategies

1. Search online digitized records at FamilySearch and Ancestry
2. Search the FamilySearch Library catalog for microfilmed church records
3. Contact the denominational archive for the relevant church body
4. Contact historical and genealogical societies in the county
5. Contact the active congregation directly — many smaller churches still hold their own records

## Key Repositories

- **FamilySearch Library** — microfilmed church records from many Kentucky congregations
- **Kentucky Historical Society** — Frankfort; manuscript church records
- **Filson Historical Society** — Louisville; holds Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian records for the Louisville area
- **Individual denominational archives** — Baptist (Southern Baptist Historical Library, Nashville), Methodist (various conference archives), Presbyterian (Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia)

getting_started.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

# Kentucky Vital Records

[U.S. Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Vital_Records "United States Vital Records")

[Kentucky](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky,_United_States_Genealogy "Kentucky, United States Genealogy")

Vital Records

## Kentucky Vital Records Dates

Years Vital Records Started in Kentucky

| **Government Registration** | **[Births](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Birth_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** | **[Marriages](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Marriage_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** | **[Deaths](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Death_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **County/Town** | 1853-1862, 1874-1878, 1892-1910 | County Formation | 1853-1862, 1874-1878, 1892-1910 |
| **Statewide Registration** | 1911 | 1958 | 1911 |
| **General Compliance** | 1917 | County Formation | 1917 |

## Background

Kentucky's vital registration history is complicated by several periods of partial compliance. Between 1852 and 1862, registration was assigned to county tax assessors who recorded events submitted by clergy, midwives, or doctors in attendance, as well as the head of household. Compliance with the law was minimal, and records were often incomplete or inaccurate. The law lapsed in 1862 during the Civil War, was briefly revived from 1874 to 1878, and again from 1892 to 1910 with poor compliance. Statewide registration began in 1911, with high compliance achieved by about 1917.

## Access Restrictions

Birth records are restricted for 100 years after the date of the event. Death records are restricted for 50 years. Marriage records are public.

## Primary Repositories

- **Kentucky Department of Public Health, Office of Vital Statistics** — statewide records from 1911 to the present
- **Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA)** — pre-1911 county-level records
- **Individual county courthouses** — marriage bonds and licenses from county formation; scattered early birth and death records

churchRecords.content:
# Kentucky Church Records

## Background

Before 1900 the largest religious groups in Kentucky were the Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, and Presbyterian churches. Church records can predate civil registration and may be the only record of baptisms, marriages, and burials for early settlers.

## Record Types

Church records may contain:
- Baptisms or christenings
- Marriage records
- Funerals or burials
- Membership lists
- Minutes or historical narratives

## Online Resources

### FamilySearch Collections
- **Kentucky Church Records, 1818–1995** — index and images (incomplete)
- **Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839–1960** — index only
- **Kentucky Marriages, 1785–1979** — index only
- **Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970** — index only

## Catholic Diocese Coverage

Kentucky is divided among four Roman Catholic dioceses: Covington, Lexington, Louisville, and Owensboro. Each diocese maintains parish-level sacramental records (baptism, marriage, burial). County assignments for each diocese are documented on the wiki.

## Research Strategies

1. Search online digitized records at FamilySearch and Ancestry
2. Search the FamilySearch Library catalog for microfilmed church records
3. Contact the denominational archive for the relevant church body
4. Contact historical and genealogical societies in the county
5. Contact the active congregation directly — many smaller churches still hold their own records

## Key Repositories

- **FamilySearch Library** — microfilmed church records from many Kentucky congregations
- **Kentucky Historical Society** — Frankfort; manuscript church records
- **Filson Historical Society** — Louisville; holds Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian records for the Louisville area
- **Individual denominational archives** — Baptist (Southern Baptist Historical Library, Nashville), Methodist (various conference archives), Presbyterian (Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia)
