question.content:
## Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records
Massachusetts has among the earliest and most complete vital records in North America. The colony mandated town recording of births, marriages, and deaths starting in 1639. Published compilations include the multi-volume 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series (known as the Tanner–Corbin series), which abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns. The Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds the original colony records, governor's correspondence, and court records from the 1620s onward. The New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) in Boston has the largest genealogical research library in New England, including manuscript collections, published genealogies, and the 'Great Migration' study series documenting every known settler who arrived 1620–1643.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records]

## Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational Church Records
Congregational church records are central to early Massachusetts genealogy. As the established church of the colony, Congregational meetings kept registers of members, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary actions (excommunications, admonishments). Many early church records have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and in local historical society publications. Land records (deeds) were recorded at the county level from the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds. Probate records begin in the 1630s at county probate courts. Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) are published and indexed separately.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational]

agent_returns.text:
Saved locality guide loc_001 for Massachusetts, 1620-1700.

---

Massachusetts was surveyed for 1620 to 1700, which covers the Plymouth Colony (founded 1620) and the Massachusetts Bay Colony (founded 1630). The strongest surviving sources are town clerk vital records, which were required from 1639, and Congregational church registers, since that church was the established one. Probate records and deeds were kept at the county level from the 1630s, and the original colony records are held at the Massachusetts Archives in Boston. The New England Historic Genealogical Society in Boston holds the largest genealogical library for the region, including the Great Migration series for settlers who arrived from 1620 to 1643. Two cautions apply. Many published town vital record compilations are abstracts rather than the originals, so check the original where one survives. The town meeting and proprietors' records from this period can only be read by browsing the images one at a time.

Next, the Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay records would need to be searched town by town, starting with the towns where a family is known to have lived.

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Oklahoma Land Records — Land Run and Homestead Records
The Land Run of 1889 and subsequent openings generated extensive federal land records. Homestead applications, final certificates, and land patents are held at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. (Record Group 49, General Land Office) and have been partially indexed on FamilySearch and the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office Records website (glorecords.blm.gov). Each homestead file typically includes the original application, proof of settlement (with witnesses), and the final patent. Rejected applications also survive and can contain family details. The Oklahoma Historical Society holds territorial and early state records, including the Oklahoma Territory census (1890 special census, one of the few surviving 1890 census records in the nation).
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run]

## Oklahoma Territorial Records — Territorial Courts and Early Settlement
Territorial court records for Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907) are at the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives. These include district court civil and criminal cases, probate, and naturalization records. Many Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states — tracing their origins often requires searching departure-state records. The first territorial census (1890) and county-level tax rolls from the 1890s help document early settlers. Church records begin sporadically in 1889 as denominations established congregations in the new towns.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts]

vitalRecords.content:
## Online Oklahoma Birth, Marriage and Death Records

### Births

* [Oklahoma State Vital Records Index](https://ok2explore.health.ok.gov/App/BirthSearch) at OK2Explore
* [Early Oklahoma Birth Records](http://sites.rootsweb.com/~okgs/early_ok_birth_records.htm) at Oklahoma Genealogical Society

### Marriages

* **1600s-1900s** [US Marriages - Oklahoma, 1600's to 1900's](https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-records/united-states-marriages?state=oklahoma) at Findmypast — index ($)
* **1870-1930** [Oklahoma Marriages, 1870-1930](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1681007) at FamilySearch — [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Marriages_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "Oklahoma Marriages - FamilySearch Historical Records"); *Also at: [Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/60105)($), [MyHeritage](http://www.myheritage.com/research/collection-30202/oklahoma-marriages-1870-1930?s=218489221)($)*
* **1889-1951** [Oklahoma County, Oklahoma Marriage Index, 1889-1951](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/9233) at Ancestry — index ($)
* **1890-1995** [Oklahoma County Marriages, 1890-1995](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1709399) at FamilySearch — [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_County_Marriages_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "Oklahoma County Marriages - FamilySearch Historical Records"); index & images; *Also at: [Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/61379)($)*
* [Oklahoma Marriage Records](https://www.okhistory.org/research/marrresults) at Oklahoma Historical Society

#### Indigenous Peoples - Marriages

* [Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Marriage, Citizenship and Census Records, 1841-1927](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/9026) ($)

### Deaths

* **1864-1941** [Oklahoma Deaths and Burials, 1864-1941](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/3518733) at FamilySearch — [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma,_Death_Records_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "Oklahoma, Death Records - FamilySearch Historical Records"); index
* [Oklahoma State Vital Records Index](https://ok2explore.health.ok.gov/App/DeathSearch) at OK2Explore

## Birth and Death Records

Some counties kept birth and death records as early as 1891, although most did not start until after statehood in 1907. The early records, which are quite incomplete, are at county courthouses. Contact details for county courts can be found on individual [county pages](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma,_United_States_Genealogy "Oklahoma, United States Genealogy"). The FamilySearch Library has copied some of the vital records of the Superintendent of Public Health in a few counties.

The statewide registration of births and deaths began in [Oklahoma](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma,_United_States_Genealogy "Oklahoma, United States Genealogy") in 1908 and was generally complied with by 1930. You can write to:

Vital Records Service  
Oklahoma State Department of Health  
1000 Northeast 10th Street, Room 111  
Oklahoma City, OK 73117  
Telephone: 405-271-4040  
[Website](https://oklahoma.gov/health/birth-and-death-certificates.html)

The current fees for obtaining copies of the state's records are listed on the Internet site above. Copies of birth records are restricted to the individual, their next of kin, or a legal representative. See the above Internet site for requirements for requesting records. Death records are not restricted.

### Accessibility to Oklahoma Birth and Death Records

Oklahoma vital records are protected by state law, 63 O.S. Sec. 1-323 (Effective Nov 1, 2016). Birth records that are at 125 years old and records of death at least 50 years old are considered open records. However, as stated on the [Oklahoma State Department of Health](https://oklahoma.gov/health/birth-and-death-certificates/genealogists.html): “…a genealogist will need written permission from the subject (if alive) or a family member if the subject is deceased. Proof of relationship between the family member and the deceased will be required.”

A list of who can request a vital record is contained on the [Oklahoma State Department of Health’s website](https://oklahoma.gov/health/birth-and-death-certificates/genealogists.html) and is also in the state law. The state does provide a free searchable index of births and deaths that occurred in the state of Oklahoma and is available at: [Ok2Explore](https://ok2explore.health.ok.gov/). If you are eligible to receive a record and want a certified copy of the record you can apply online through a [partner website](https://www.vitalchek.com/vital-records/oklahoma/oklahoma-vital-records?click_id=646266980319952898&ppc=0) or by phone (or mail) to the Vital Records Service. You will have to pick up the record in Oklahoma City and provide proof of eligibility to receive the record.

### Delayed Birth Records

Delayed registrations of births (for persons born before registration began in 1908) are available from the Vital Records Service mentioned above.

## Marriage Records

Before 1890, no marriages were recorded by the county or state. 1830's to 1889 very few records exist, some recorded in district courts.

Oklahoma became a state in 1907. Prior to statehood it was Indian Territory from the 1830's to 1890. In 1890 Oklahoma was divided into two Territories (Twin Territories) Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory.

In 1890 three Judicial Districts were established where marriages could be performed and recorded:

* First District: at Muskogee included Cherokee and Creek Nations
* Second District: at South McAlester included Choctaw Nation

# Locality Guide: Land Run of 1889 settlers (Oklahoma Territory, 1889 to statehood in 1907) (1889-1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory was created in 1890 from the western part of the Indian Territory split (the Twin Territories); the state was admitted in 1907. The survey did not confirm the exact formation statute.
- **County seat / administrative center:** not confirmed by this survey.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (territory, then state from 1907).
- **Population during period:** the survey returned no population figures.
- **Economy:** not confirmed by this survey.
- **Ethnic composition:** not confirmed by this survey; the wiki notes many settlers came from Kansas, Texas and Missouri.
- **Religious denominations:** not confirmed; the wiki says church congregations began sporadically in 1889.
- **Key historical events:** the 1889 Land Run and later openings (FamilySearch Wiki, Oklahoma Land Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Coverage of this survey:** the volumes part lists 2 image groups in total, and both are listed. The Catalog returned no hits.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1890, the area was Indian Territory. In 1890 it was divided into Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory (FamilySearch Wiki, Oklahoma Vital Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records).
- The 1889 Land Run opened land that the wiki places in Oklahoma Territory. Records from 1889 may therefore sit in territorial files, while earlier Indian Territory records sit with the Indian Territory courts and the Muskogee and South McAlester marriage districts.
- Oklahoma became a state in 1907. The survey did not confirm any county-level boundary changes for the period.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the Land Run homestead files. The Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records collection (1541872, 1834-1907) is online and is the fastest route to a claimant. Then check the national land files in the National Archives Record Group 49 and the glorecords.blm.gov index (FamilySearch Wiki, Oklahoma Land Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run). Next, use the Oklahoma County Marriages collection (2134789, from 1890) and the Oklahoma Deaths and Burials collection (3518733, 1864-1941). The Dawes enrollment jackets are browse-only and should come last.
- Homestead files usually include the application, witnessed proof of settlement and final patent. Rejected applications also survive and can name family members (FamilySearch Wiki, Oklahoma Land Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- Vital records: statewide registration began in 1908. Some counties kept incomplete birth and death records from 1891 at the county courthouse (FamilySearch Wiki, Oklahoma Vital Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records).
- Territorial courts: district court civil, criminal, probate and naturalization records for 1890-1907 are at the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives (FamilySearch Wiki, Oklahoma Territorial Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- Many settlers came from Kansas, Texas and Missouri. Search departure-state records as well (FamilySearch Wiki, Oklahoma Territorial Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- Naming conventions: not confirmed by this survey.
- Alternative sources: the wiki points to the 1890 special Oklahoma Territory census at the Oklahoma Historical Society, and to county tax rolls from the 1890s.
- Finding aids: the Oklahoma Historical Society and the National Archives are the named repositories. The survey's Catalog returned no hits, so check the catalog directly.

---

**Alabama Before Statehood (~1800): Locality Research Guide**

**Jurisdictional Context**
The area that became Alabama was part of the **Mississippi Territory** (1798–1817), then briefly the **Alabama Territory** (1817–1819) before statehood in 1819. The Mobile/south Alabama area also has a layered colonial history under French, British, and Spanish rule.

**Surviving Record Types for This Period**
- **Territorial censuses**: 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 — held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery

The survey found **no digitized, browsable image volumes** for Alabama or the Mississippi Territory on FamilySearch — not even unindexed ones. This is a gap in what could be confirmed online, not necessarily proof they don't exist.

Contact the **Alabama Department of Archives and History** (Montgomery) directly — they are the primary repository for territorial-era records and may have digitized volumes or microfilm not yet surfaced online.

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records
Alabama was part of the Mississippi Territory from 1798 to 1817, then became the Alabama Territory until statehood in 1819. Territorial records include land grants, tax lists, militia rolls, and court records. The earliest land records are Spanish and British colonial grants in the Mobile area. The Mississippi Territory census of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These territorial censuses are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records]

## Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records
Before American control, the Mobile area was administered by France (1702-1763), Britain (1763-1780), and Spain (1780-1813). French colonial records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence and in microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish records of the Mobile District include census returns, church registers, and land grants held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records]

Alabama was part of the Mississippi Territory from 1798 to 1817, then became the Alabama Territory until statehood in 1819. Territorial records include land grants, tax lists, militia rolls, and court records. The earliest land records are Spanish and British colonial grants in the Mobile area. The Mississippi Territory census of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These territorial censuses are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records]

## Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records
Before American control, the Mobile area was administered by France (1702-1763), Britain (1763-1780), and Spain (1780-1813). French colonial records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence and in microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish records of the Mobile District include census returns, church registers, and land grants held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records]

I also ran a separate survey under the Mississippi Territory name, which found the same absence of volumes; I did not save it as its own entry.

The next step is for you to check the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery for the territorial census and any digitized territorial volumes, since this search could not confirm any online.

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Pennsylvania Coal Region Records — Overview
The Pennsylvania Coal Region Records page gathers specialized indexes for the anthracite counties (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, Carbon) that sit alongside the standard civil records. It describes colliery employment indexes drawn from company payroll books, coal-region Catholic parish survival, and the triennial state tax assessments — sources unique to the anthracite field. See the full page for the specific index titles and their coverage years.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]

## Pennsylvania Coal Region Records — Choosing an index
Anthracite-region researchers should distinguish company payroll indexes (which name individual colliery workers) from mine-inspection and accident reports (which are organized by colliery, not by person). Payroll-derived indexes are the more direct genealogical finding aid for immigrant miners whose names were indexed inconsistently in census records.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]

---

## Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide (c. 1770–1791)

### Jurisdictional Background

Vermont before statehood (1791) sat in a contested zone — both **New York** and **New Hampshire** claimed sovereignty over the territory. Because of this overlap, records from this period may be held under any of three governments:

- The **Republic of Vermont** (self-declared independent 1777–1791)
- **New York** colonial/state government
- **New Hampshire** colonial/state government

This means you may need to search record repositories in all three jurisdictions, not just Vermont.

### Key Record Source: 1771 Grant Survey Schedule

The FamilySearch Wiki's Vermont place page documents a **1771 Grant Survey Schedule**, prepared under New York authority, that lists approximately **1,800 grantees** of the disputed New Hampshire grants. If your ancestor held a land grant in Vermont before statehood, this schedule may name them.

### Record Availability Cautions

- **Statewide civil registration** (births, marriages, deaths) did not begin in Vermont until **1857**.
- Pre-1791 town clerk records **survive unevenly** — coverage depends on the specific town.
- **Town clerk offices** are the primary repositories for any earlier vital or land records that do survive.
- No digitized FamilySearch collections, image volumes, or catalog entries were confirmed for pre-1791 Vermont in this survey.

### Suggested Next Steps

1. Identify which Vermont town(s) your ancestor lived in and contact that town clerk's office directly for surviving pre-1791 records.
2. Search New York and New Hampshire colonial records, since those governments administered the territory before 1791.
3. Consult the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule for any land-grant connections.
4. Build a formal research plan starting from this guide once your ancestor's town is identified.

---

*The guide notes that digitized FamilySearch collections for this period remain unconfirmed, so brick-wall research here will likely require off-FamilySearch sources (state archives, town clerks, New York and New Hampshire repositories).*

home.content:
# Vermont Genealogy

Vermont, the 14th state (admitted 1791), has a distinctive set of pre-statehood land records that researchers should not confuse with later post-statehood records.

## Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule
The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule, prepared under New York colonial authority before statehood, enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Each entry lists grantee, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. This record predates any Vermont civil registration and is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state.

## Civil Vital Records
Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857. Earlier town clerk records (some back to the 1770s) survive unevenly; consult town clerk offices directly.

## Town Histories
Nineteenth-century town histories (most published 1860-1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access.

question.content:
## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

vitalRecords.content:
# England Civil Registration

Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths in England and Wales began on **1 July 1837**. Before this date, no civil birth certificates exist — the primary sources for births before 1837 are Anglican parish registers recording baptisms.

## Registration Start Date

The Registration Act 1836 established the system of civil registration that came into force on 1 July 1837. The General Register Office (GRO) was established to oversee registration.

## Before Civil Registration (before 1 July 1837)

For events before 1837, the main alternatives are:

- **Anglican parish registers** — recording baptisms (not births), marriages, and burials. The oldest date from the 1530s.
- **Bishop's transcripts** — annual copies of parish registers sent to the diocesan bishop, often surviving where original registers do not.
- **Nonconformist records** — Baptists, Methodists, Quakers, and other dissenting congregations kept their own registers. Many were deposited at the General Register Office in 1837 and are now at the National Archives (RG 4–8).

## Early Registration (1837–1875)

Early civil registration was incomplete. The requirement to register was established in law, but enforcement was weak in the early years. Many births, deaths, and marriages were never registered. Parish records remain essential even after 1837 for this reason.

## Finding Civil Registration Records

Civil registration indexes (organized quarterly from 1837) are the finding aid for GRO records. Indexes are available at:
- **FreeBMD** (free, volunteer-transcribed)
- **Findmypast** (subscription)
- **Ancestry** (subscription)
- **GRO Historical Indexes** (gov.uk, free for births and deaths 1837–1957)

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the England and Wales Death Registration Index 1837-2007 (collection 2285341), which is free to search on FamilySearch and covers 1851 deaths. - Anglican parish registers and bishop's transcripts are the main burial sources for 1851; the survey did not confirm which Yorkshire parishes' registers survive for 1851.
- Regional and commercial indexes to check: Yorkshire Births Marriages & Deaths Indexes (http://www.yorkshirebmd.org.uk/) and Findmypast's Yorkshire Parish Registers and Bishop's Transcripts browse (http://search.findmypast.co.uk/search-world-Records/yorkshire-parish-registers-and-bishops-transcripts-browse), which is subscription-based.
- Nonconformist registers were deposited at the GRO in 1837 and are now at The National Archives (RG 4-8), per the England Civil Registration page.
- Search the death index by name and year 1851; the survey did not confirm any 1851 census collection for Yorkshire, so use the death indexes and burial registers as the primary sources.

## Boundary changes
- The survey did not return boundary changes for Yorkshire during or near 1851.
- Civil death registration for England and Wales began 1 July 1837 under the General Register Office (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration), so the 1851 death falls within the civil registration period, though enforcement was weak in the early years.
- Boundaries stated as stable: not confirmed by this survey.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the England and Wales Death Registration Index 1837-2007 (collection 2285341), which is free to search on FamilySearch and covers 1851 deaths. Next, search FreeBMD and the GRO Historical Indexes (free) for the same death to get the registration quarter and district. Then search the Yorkshire parish burial registers (collection 4439317, England, Yorkshire, Parish Registers, 1538-2016) and England, Deaths and Burials, 1538-1991 (collection 1473016) by parish, since an unregistered death will appear only in the burial register.
- Civil registration of deaths began 1 July 1837 and enforcement was weak early on, so a missing civil index entry does not prove the death did not occur (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration).
- Anglican parish registers and bishop's transcripts are the main burial sources for 1851; the survey did not confirm which Yorkshire parishes' registers survive for 1851.
- Regional and commercial indexes to check: Yorkshire Births Marriages & Deaths Indexes (http://www.yorkshirebmd.org.uk/) and Findmypast's Yorkshire Parish Registers and Bishop's Transcripts browse (http://search.findmypast.co.uk/search-world-Records/yorkshire-parish-registers-and-bishops-transcripts-browse), which is subscription-based.
- Nonconformist registers were deposited at the GRO in 1837 and are now at The National Archives (RG 4-8), per the England Civil Registration page.
- Search the death index by name and year 1851; the survey did not confirm any 1851 census collection for Yorkshire, so use the death indexes and burial registers as the primary sources.
